data.title: Britain must maintain its lead to unlock energy’s holy grail
data.description:
It’s long been the “somewhere over the rainbow” promise of economic transformation that never seems to arrive. No, I’m not talking about AI, which, though already with us, has yet to prove the grandiose claims made of it.

Rather, I’m referring to nuclear fusion. This is the holy grail of energy production – the promise of limitless quantities of low-cost, carbon-free, baseload electricity.

Like the grail itself, commercialisation has thus far eluded even the world’s finest scientific minds and entrepreneurs.

But that doesn’t mean it’s still just science fiction. Lab-made fusion has already been successfully demonstrated on multiple occasions, and the science behind it is now relatively well advanced.

Yet until a few years ago, all such experimentation consumed more power than it generated, rendering it useless as an energy source.

As the old joke goes, economically viable fusion is about 30 years away, and will always be 30 years away. Harnessing the same power as the sun has proved much more difficult in practice than in theory.

In the past several years, however, there have been some very definite signs of the required breakthroughs.

And perhaps surprisingly, some of them are happening in Britain. With its history of academic excellence, the UK has always been good at this sort of stuff, but it has also been notably poor at commercialising it.

Innovative success has not translated well into economic exploitation. Rather, it is the US, and increasingly China, that tend to capitalise on what comes out of British brainpower.

Is fusion likely to suffer the same fate?

Dennis Whyte, who was this month appointed the chief executive of the UK Atomic Energy Authority – the Government body responsible for the nation’s “fusion strategy” – is determined that it should not. Formerly director of the fusion centre at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Whyte believes the UK has a unique set of capabilities that will allow it to excel in fusion’s development and commercialisation.

But first let’s talk about the potential, which to economic nerds like me is the really interesting bit.

Move over AI, the truly transformational technology coming down the road at us is not fully conscious humanoid robots but fusion.

Most economic progress is at root about energy and our ability to harness it to human purposes. At the heart of the industrial revolution, for instance, was not so much the machines themselves as the transformative power of coal.

The so-called Kardashev scale, though in some respects quack science, provides one way of charting economic advancement according to energy consumption.

Named after Nikolai Kardashev, the Soviet era astronomer, it seeks to measure progress in civilisation based entirely on the amount of energy that can be harnessed and deployed.

According to Kardashev, it’s only when humans manage to access unlimited quantities of it beyond mere Earth-bound sources that civilisation achieves its true potential.

This may or may not be an endorsement, but Elon Musk is particularly keen on the Kardashev way of thinking.

Only for him it’s about accessing the power of the sun via solar panels, battery storage and infrastructure in space. Indeed, he has dismissed pursuit of Earth-bound fusion reactors as “super dumb and farcical”.

Musk is the undisputed master of tech commercialisation, so he has to be taken seriously. Nonetheless, he should know better than anyone that progress involves, through a process of trial and error, testing the frontiers of science to virtual destruction and eventually finding a way through.

Think about it; if manmade fusion can be achieved at scale, it is likely to be a far bigger driver of productivity growth than anything AI can offer, as well as being a potential solution to any existential threat posed by climate change.

As Whyte points out, AI is a technology with unproven potential, despite the hundreds of billions of dollars being invested in it.

A lot of questions remain about its supposedly transformational powers, as last week’s wobble in AI-related stocks and shares seemed to confirm.

Nobody knows what its effect on jobs and growth might be, still less whether it is capable of generating the returns needed to justify the vast amounts being invested in it.

With energy, on the other hand, we already know what cheap power can do; fusion is moreover not just a further time-limited energy source, in the same way as a new gas field might be.

It is a forever, unlimited resource that promises to power hitherto undreamt levels of technological advancement and human progress. If it can be achieved, it truly would be a game changer, and as an economic leap forward, perhaps bigger than even the Industrial Revolution.

Interestingly, it is also complementary to the development of AI, which both has an insatiable appetite for power and whose computational skills are already helping to turbo-charge the pursuit of commercially viable fusion.

There is a developing symbiosis between the two, a mutually beneficial co-dependency which ought to help both technologies achieve their potential.

I’m no expert, so I cannot tell you if in 30 years’ time we’ll still be saying fusion is 30 years away and will always be 30 years away.

But Whyte knows as much as there is to know about fusion, and he’s never been more optimistic.

A growing number of labs and companies are successfully achieving it, including recently General Fusion Group, which has announced that its magnetised target fusion (MTF) technology has reached electron temperatures exceeding 12 million degrees Celsius, well in advance of what’s needed for fusion to take place.

The results were confirmed using the UK Atomic Energy Authority measurement techniques.

What’s more, around £10bn of private capital globally has been invested in fusion in a clear signal that commercialisation is beginning to be seen as eminently possible and even likely.

Not to be outdone, China is also chasing hard, having elevated fusion to a core strategic frontier and national infrastructure priority.

Some readers may be familiar with an Apple TV science fiction series called For All Mankind, which is based around the idea that the space race never ended.

The consequent superpower rivalry drives rapid technological progress, such that by the year 2000 space exploration and colonisation are far in advance of anything we see today.

The same rivalry already apparent between the West and China in AI is beginning to take hold in nuclear fusion, where China has a significant advantage in terms of the supply chains and manufacturing capacity needed to make fusion reactors a reality.

Still, Britain is for now very much part of the race. The UK was the first country in the world to produce nuclear power at scale for civilian use. It would be nice to think it is still capable of doing the same with fusion.

data.title: Poundland owner to avoid scrutiny in closed-door session before MPs
data.description:
Poundland’s owners have been granted permission to give evidence to MPs in a rare closed-door session.

Mark Newton-Jones, the European head of US investor Gordon Brothers, was asked to appear before the Commons business committee next week to face questions about the future of the discount chain.

However, it is understood Mr Newton-Jones requested that the session be held in private to avoid a “show trial” that could harm the chances of a successful sale of the business.

The fate of up to 12,000 jobs has been left hanging in the balance after Gordon Brothers – described by Jonathan Brash, the MP for Hartlepool, as “predatory capitalists” – filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators in the High Court last week.

The move has been widely criticised after Gordon Brothers rejected a takeover offer from Martin Property Group.

Liam Byrne, the Labour MP who chairs the all-party select committee, demanded that Mr Newton-Jones face questions at a session on Nov 11, calling the situation a “matter of significant interest”.

However, he has since acceded to a request from the former Mothercare chief to exclude the public from the hearing.

In a statement, he said: “Since we asked Gordon Brothers to appear before Parliament, we’ve been in daily contact and we understand they are now in active talks with several credible buyers about selling Poundland as a going concern.

“We want those talks to succeed and we want to understand what I know will be highly sensitive commercial information in detail.

“Given the assurances that Gordon Brothers are now focused on a sale of the active business that will save jobs and stores, we will permit them to appear before the committee in private session in the first instance and issue a statement of our findings thereafter.”

It is understood that Martin Property Group is still in talks about a potential deal with Gordon Brothers, which has also received an offer from Xyra Group Holdings, a little-known London investment firm.

Restructuring firm AlixPartners has been put on standby to handle Poundland’s insolvency if a credible sale deal cannot be secured.

Gordon Brothers bought Poundland only in June last year, at the time promising to provide “the financing to support the substantial turnaround of this iconic retailer”, which has a network of more than 600 stores.

In a statement this week, Gordon Brothers said: “We are pursuing all avenues through the sale process to find a solution which protects as many jobs as possible and preserves value.

“In spite of our efforts and the tremendous efforts of management to deliver a turnaround, the business remains challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading.”

Gordon Brothers was contacted for comment.

data.title: ‘China Shock 2.0’ is crushing the West
data.description:
Robot vacuum cleaners are typically less noisy than their older, hand-operated cousins. But the volume of the Chinese-made versions is not the only quiet thing. They are also stealthily taking over the world.

Dreame, a company founded in Suzhou less than a decade ago, is now said to be the world’s biggest seller of robot vacuums. Its founder, 39-year-old Yu Hao, claims to be building a $100tn (£75tn) ecosystem of smart appliances and frontier tech.

After just two years in Britain, Dreame is still a relatively small player here. Euromonitor International put the company’s UK market share at 4pc last year.

But four Chinese companies control almost half the UK market. And their cheapest products are all priced below those of SharkNinja and Dyson, which manufacture in Asia but do at least some of the brain-work in the US and Britain, respectively.

When it comes to Chinese imports, most people think first of electric vehicles (EVs), which are swarming into markets worldwide, such as Jaecoo, a brand that has become the go-to for British consumers. It is certainly the prime battlefront, with Britain under growing pressure to mimic the EU’s tariffs of up to 45pc on EVs.

Beneath these headlines, however, cut-price Chinese imports of just about any manufactured product are now sweeping into the West and challenging local businesses.

Consumers love the low prices. But companies and governments across Europe now fear that the Chinese juggernaut will hoover up Western industries and jobs, and leave the Continent utterly dependent on the whims and will of Beijing.

The timing of this “China Shock 2.0” – the first shock was the flood of low-priced toys, clothes and other manufactured goods that hit in the early 2000s – is not a coincidence. In the past few years, Beijing has unmuzzled its most potent weapon to win the export war.

Chinese factories have long enjoyed advantages such as cheap workers and raw materials, generous subsidies and massive economies of scale. But now a new wave of cheap credit – that is, loans made on concessional or non-commercial terms – has swept through the Chinese manufacturing sector, unlocking the export tsunami.

“This is probably the single biggest component of China’s industrial policy,” says Camille Boullenois, a China expert at the Rhodium Group consultancy.

“It has been the most powerful and the most influential factor shaping the economic system in China, because the entire economic system is based on credit.”

‘Everything in China is political’

Ever since China’s banks pulled back from lending to households after the spectacular property crash of 2021, they have been scrambling to find enough borrowers.

And with the Chinese government ever more focused on ramping up high-tech and advanced manufacturing, that’s where the banks have been pouring all that surplus cash.

“There’s a natural herding in the way the Chinese private sector operates. Once everybody realised that manufacturing is where the political light was shining, then capital and human talent moved into manufacturing,” says David Lubin, of the think tank Chatham House.

The banks have become the pivotal enabler of Beijing’s ambition to ensure companies, such as Dreame, dominate global markets and supply chains.

“Lending is political, because everything in China is political. And credit is a political tool,” says Leo Austin, a businessman who advises multinationals on working in China.

These dirt-cheap loans mean that, unlike their Western rivals, many Chinese companies can receive capital on tap.

“There is always cash flow available to you, and you have no short-term fear around the viability of the business, so you can afford to be incredibly aggressive,” Austin says.

This has wrought a transformation in China that is little appreciated outside its borders.

Once there were private firms and state-owned enterprises. But now most companies are a hybrid: they have a private-sector management culture, but are almost entirely funded by government-sourced equity and state-backed lending.

Austin calls this model “state-capitalised private enterprises”. The emerging Chinese high-tech giants are almost all cut from this cloth.

Chinese banks are bound by law to lend money “in accordance with the needs of the national economic and social development, and under the guidance of the industrial policies of the state”.

And they do. Beijing’s corporate debt totals about 138pc of GDP, almost double the ratio in the US. But Chinese companies’ interest costs amount to less than 1pc of turnover, compared with 5pc for their American peers.

The effect of this fresh wave of cheap credit has been immediate.

China’s domination

Between 2021 and 2024, the number of products where China accounts for more than half of global exports nearly doubled, from 192 to 315.

China’s trade surplus will again surpass $1tn this year. The surplus with both Germany and France has doubled in the past year. For the EU as a whole, it amounts to more than €1bn (£840m) a day.

Although this export surge makes China appear like a rising economic superpower, the boom in cheap credit and factory exports has a dark side.

Companies are exporting their credit-fuelled output because Chinese households, burnt by the property crash, are not spending. At home, Chinese companies are forced into painful discounting wars just to move stock.

Profitability has plummeted and one in three companies is loss-making. Without the exports, which often provide more than 40pc of revenue, many businesses would be unviable.

Yet the banks keep lending and lending. Often, they have to discount the interest rate simply because otherwise the borrower would go bust.

Instead, it is European competitors who are absorbing the blow. In Britain, some have complained to the Trade Remedies Authority (TRA), which can impose quotas or tariffs.

The TRA has sought to protect local manufacturers from cut-price Chinese imports of everything from ceramics to ironing boards, tyres and cherry-pickers.

One recent TRA ruling noted that Chinese companies “have access to preferential financing, and access to financing from institutions which implement public policy objectives or otherwise do not act independently of the state”.

The TRA added: “They have more flexibility and can adjust their business and pricing strategies to maximise their export sales and gain market share in the UK, even if they would have otherwise made negative profit margins.”

No easy answers

Given that the Government is aware of the problem, many businesses want to see it push back harder. “There are probably plenty of stones that could be unturned,” one industry veteran says.

Rhodium’s Boullenois says the same is true in Europe, where Brussels’s trade directorate is overwhelmed with business requests for protection.

“We’re protecting too few products. Our defences need to be much broader, and work much faster,” she says.

But if the EU and US protect their own markets, more of the ultra-cheap Chinese exports will simply shift to Asia, Africa and Latin America – displacing European and American rivals in those countries’ markets.

“We normally look at how much is China selling to the EU. A lot less time is spent thinking about how many EU products the Chinese manufacturers are displacing in foreign markets – and it’s huge,” says Joe Peissel, of the consultancy Trivium China.

The battle against China’s factories is on in earnest. But as long as the Chinese are backed up by the bazooka of the country’s banking system, it will be a war that the West will struggle to win.

data.title: Parking fines capped at £100 in purge on ‘cowboys’
data.description:
Parking penalties are to be capped at £100 as Andy Burnham cracks down on so-called “cowboy” companies.

Motorists will also be given 10 minutes to leave car parks without facing a penalty once their paid-for time is up, under new legally binding rules due to come into force by the end of the year.

The Private Parking Code of Practice will give drivers the right to have charges cancelled on appeal for honest mistakes.

These include a breakdown in a car park, a medical emergency or a broken ticket machine, as well as stopping briefly to check directions and issues outside the driver’s control.

Mr Burnham said: “Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn’t end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.

“These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I’m putting a stop to them.

“We are introducing clearer rules, longer grace periods and lower charges for genuine mistakes, while going after the deliberate scams that rip drivers off.”

Under the code, drivers who make mistakes such as forgetting parking permits, entering a vehicle registration wrong or forgetting to confirm it in a parking machine, will face a maximum charge of £20, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said.

At present, Westminster council, for example, issues penalties of up to £130. These increase to £195 for a single contravention if not paid within 14 days.

Simon Williams, the RAC’s head of policy, said the code was a “step in the right direction” to protect drivers from the practices of some private parking companies, but “not the leap” the motoring services company had been campaigning for.

He said: “We’ve long called for the banning of debt recovery fees being added on top of parking charge notices and a single independent appeals body to replace the two industry-run ones, but neither have been included, which is disappointing.

“That said, the fact we finally have a code seven years on from the Private Parking Code of Practice Act becoming law is positive.”

A similar parking code of practice was issued in 2022 by the Conservative government. The parking industry robustly challenged it, prompting that set of rules to be withdrawn almost straight away.

Yet over-aggressive parking enforcement has been one of the nation’s biggest bugbears for many years.

In 2017, a Scottish woman was given a £24,500 penalty after ignoring more than 200 penalties, while in 2025 a nurse was taken to court by a private parking company after she “repeatedly” took more than five minutes after entering the car park to buy a ticket.

Will Hurley, the chief executive of the International Parking Community trade body, said: “I genuinely hope the new code is a good thing for the industry. We’ve put so much work into making sure that the Government understands the importance of it.

“For years I’ve been trying to change this mindset within the sector,” he added.

“Instead of looking for a reason to issue a charge, or instead of looking for a reason to reject an appeal [against a parking penalty], look for a reason not to issue a charge, or look for a reason to cancel a parking charge on appeal. And it’s just a slightly different mindset that I genuinely think makes a difference.”

A record 16.9 million parking tickets were handed out by private businesses in the 12 months to the end of March, according to analysis of government data by the Press Association and the RAC Foundation.

That is up from 14.4 million the year before, and 6.8 million in 2018-19. The parking industry attributed the rise to an increase in the number of car parks being managed.

Each ticket can be up to £100, meaning the total cost to drivers may be more than £4.6m per day at the current rate.

Alison Tooze, chief policy officer at the British Parking Association, said the new code was an “an important step forward for motorists, communities and responsible parking operators”.

“Overall, the code strikes the right balance between stronger protections for motorists and effective parking management, helping keep communities, businesses and local economies moving,” she said.

Jack Cousens, the head of roads policy at the AA, said: “After seven long years, drivers finally have something which could offer them better protections against the worst private parking operators. For too long, many private parking operators have aggressively attacked drivers to the point where many simply pay up if they receive a charge from one on the doorstep.

“While this is a good first step, there is still a huge amount of work to do, such as tackling the scourge of debt recovery fees. Ultimately, we need to stop charges being issued in the first place, especially where the driver has done nothing wrong.”

data.title: Burnham’s crackdown on headphone-dodgers ‘impossible to enforce’
data.description:
Labour’s plan to fine bus passengers £100 for playing music out loud will be impossible to implement without recruiting a costly army of enforcement officials, industry bosses warned.

Only a handful of local authorities have their own transport safety officers trained in tackling antisocial behaviour, while there are no plans to involve bus drivers in the campaign.

Alison Edwards, of the Confederation of Passenger Transport, said bus firms backed the crackdown but that the success of the scheme will “come down to budgets”.

She said: “We welcome the recognition that it’s an issue and the powers to tackle that, but what they need now is the ability to enforce that meaningfully.

“There’s a question mark because there’s a cost involved. Have they got the funding to have transport safety offices where they need them?”

She added: “Bus drivers are not security guards and it would be wrong to expect them to enforce the law.”

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, launched the campaign on headphone-dodgers last week, saying that “blasting music or videos” gets on people’s nerves “and can quickly spoil the journey”.

The campaign builds on legislation introduced last year giving local leaders new powers to tackle loud music, vaping and littering on buses, backed by the threat of a £100 penalty.

Antisocial behaviour on trains can attract £1,000 fines, enforceable by the British Transport Police, which works only on the railway, even though buses attract more passengers.

Phil Southall, a managing director at Go-Ahead, which runs buses throughout England, said he was “sceptical” about the scheme given the funding crisis at local authorities.

He said: “The Government says the responsibility for enforcing this falls to councils. But if the councils haven’t got the resources then nothing’s going to change.

“The bus drivers won’t do it because they’re not required to. If they don’t feel safe they’re not going to get out of the cab, and they’re certainly not going to be levying the fines.

“We will brief them on the change in legislation but the briefing will be ‘it’s not your responsibility’, basically.”

He added: “The whole definition probably needs a bit of clarity, too. A grandmother playing a TikTok video because she forgot her headphones, is that the same as a load of yobs?”

Metroline, which operates mostly in London, said that while eliminating antisocial behaviour was a long-term goal, the scarcity of funding meant the industry needed to pick its targets.

Using mobile phones on loudspeaker is a ‘low-level’ concern

Sean O’Shea, the chief commercial officer at parent group ComfortDelGro, said: “There aren’t those huge resources that would enable us to cover the whole spectrum. I don’t know if it’s going to end up being that big a priority.

“In terms of the hierarchy, violence against women and girls is far more important. If we can tackle the big issues and crack that, then let’s work our way down the list.”

He said habits such as people using mobile phones on loudspeaker might be seen as antisocial but were “low level and just something that people do because the technology enables it”.

Greater Manchester’s Bee Network, established when Mr Burnham was mayor, is one of the few bus services with a fully fledged enforcement operation, partly funded with government grants for which it became eligible after pioneering a London-style franchising model.

The city has 150 enforcement officers who respond to everything from drunks on buses and trams to violent disorder.

Even then, resources are spread thinly, with the force split into three divisions, each working four shifts to target the morning rush, end of the school day, evening drinkers and night buses.

Kate Green, the head of policing and community safety at Transport for Greater Manchester, said a live police chat room for concerned passengers currently redirects reports of vaping, smoking and noise away from a police response.

She said: “We patrol those routes and warn people they’ll have to leave if their behaviour continues. There’s no fine, but I do wonder how much that is going to change.”

The Department for Transport said those local authorities that elect to take up the new powers will also be responsible for their enforcement.

data.title: Rayner on track to deliver fewer homes than the Tories
data.description:
Labour is on track to deliver fewer homes this parliament than the Conservatives in a setback for Angela Rayner, the Housing Secretary.

A total of 1.14 million homes are expected to be added to Britain’s housing stock in the five years of this parliament, according to fresh forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

That is fewer than the nearly 1.18 million built in the 2019-24 parliament, which was cut short by an early election. The period of Conservative rule was also blighted by the pandemic lockdowns that shut down building sites.

The forecast from the OBR is a blow for Ms Rayner and Labour, which has made boosting housebuilding a key priority.

In its 2024 manifesto, Labour criticised the Conservatives for failing to build enough homes and promised to “get Britain building again”. The party vowed to deliver 1.5 million new homes over this parliament.

Industry has long warned that the Government is well off track to meet this goal but ministers have continued to defend it.

Ms Rayner described it as a “really difficult stretch target” in July but insisted the goal was not being dropped. In September, she admitted there was only a “slim chance” of building 1.5 million new homes but said: “I’m definitely not giving it up.”

The Housing Secretary has sought to blame the Iran war for blowing the Government off course, saying rising interest rates have weighed on the housing market.

However, Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, blamed the Government for the backwards step on home construction.

Ms Lam said: “Labour have no excuse. They’ve utterly failed to bring their pledge to fruition because they’ve layered taxes and red tape on to the industry, making building less and less viable.”

Steve Turner, the executive director of the Home Builders Federation, said Labour’s reforms since taking office were welcome but failed to address “the massive increase over the past 20 years in the level of taxation and policies, all with a cost, levied on to housebuilding by successive governments”.

These included requirements to build more affordable homes as well as environmental schemes and taxes, he said, adding that “demand is suppressed by a lack of affordable mortgage lending”.

The average five-year fixed mortgage currently available comes with an interest rate of almost 5.9pc, according to Moneyfacts, up from 4.9pc before the war in Iran began at the end of February.

John Healey, the Chancellor, has instructed Andrew Bailey, the Governor of the Bank of England, to seek more ways to help first-time buyers.

In a letter sent last week to set out the mandate of the Bank’s financial policy committee, Mr Healey called for the Bank to “target improving access to home ownership without prejudicing financial stability”, urging officials to look at rules around high loan-to-value mortgages.

Such mortgages are often taken by those buyers making their first step on to the housing ladder, requiring an initial loan which is relatively large compared to their earnings.

In forecasts produced alongside the Budget, the OBR cut its projection for house building during the coming five years by 190,000.

The watchdog said it still believed Labour’s reforms would “have a positive impact on housebuilding” but said the downgrade reflected “wider pressures in the construction sector because of weak demand, rising material costs and the impact of other regulatory changes”.

A spokesman for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “We’re getting this country building again and with new housing starts up 20pc compared to this time last year, and a 298pc increase in London alone, our bold planning reforms are working.

“We’ve always been clear that delivering 1.5 million homes was a stretch target and we recognise the challenges the sector is facing with construction costs and macro-economic headwinds.”

data.title: Supermarket fridge hacks are a dire warning for Britain’s grid
data.description:
In his 2020 book Apocalypse How?, Oliver Letwin, the former Tory minister, imagines a doomsday scenario where Britain’s electricity grid collapses, taking down everything that relies on an internet connection.

His chilling message was straightforward.

The system that controls the electricity grid and the internet cannot be divorced, and in racing towards a low-carbon system for power generation, we have lost the capacity to quickly bring the grid – and our Wi-Fi systems – back online after a blackout.

It was reading his book as light relief in the first wave of the Covid pandemic that made me “dumb down” our smart home.

But it doesn’t take an apocalyptic book to see the future. The electricity grid is already creaking without anyone hacking it.

The vulnerabilities of our internet-powered economy are already top of mind after the widespread supermarket-fridge hacks across Europe.

Hackers turned off the cooling on fridges at more than 700 French supermarkets last month.

On Monday, it happened again.

In Sweden, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Estonia and Ireland, the temperature of network-connected fridges was turned up and food was ruined.

So far, so wasteful. A one-off was a curiosity. But twice in a month is a pattern, and shows the fears that Letwin originally put his finger on: the precariousness of our connected world.

In Britain we have an added vulnerability: the electricity grid itself.

Take, for example, the bizarre energy-balancing system required to keep the lights on.

Britain recently asked France for 1,200 megawatts of “last resort” energy to help shore up the power needs of London and the south east, while also paying wind farms in Scotland to switch off because the wires were overloaded.

And when it goes wrong, it goes really wrong. The grid can’t just be switched back on. Restarting the system requires generating stations that can start without power from the grid.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso) is the grid’s system operator and legally required to have the capability to restore 60pc of demand within 24 hours in every region of Great Britain.

Three years ago its own modelling put the time at just more than 32 hours. Whether they can meet their obligation, nobody has said.

On a sweltering evening in June the grid’s frequency fell below its operating limits.

Neso said the system was “not at risk”, but a whistleblower alleged records were massaged to hide how close it came.

An independent investigation found no evidence for a cover-up, revealing instead executives who did not fully understand their own control room and a culture of “reputational sensitivity” passed down to the engineers.

We have seen far too many times what happens when the people at the top are more fluent in reassurance than in reality. It does not end well.

As for the operators in Britain’s complex energy system, the “smart money” is already finding a way around the constraints of the grid by simply circumventing it.

Drax announced this week it would develop a data centre at its North Yorkshire power station with Canadian giant Brookfield and the fund’s AI platform Radiant.

Drax isn’t really selling land development. It’s selling a four-gigawatt (GW) grid connection and a wood-burning power station whose vital state subsidies are set to be cut next year and run out in 2031.

The tech bros have been ahead in the off-grid game for some time.

AI is enormously power hungry, and data centres are winning the race for power.

There are currently 140 proposed data centres seeking grid connections, requiring roughly 50GW, more than the entire country uses at its winter peak.

In west London, new homes are already delayed because data centres secured the spare capacity first.

The irony is that old thermal sites like Drax are exactly what a restoration plan for the grid relies on to restart, and exactly what AI companies now want to buy.

Either data centres with their own generation become islands that help restart the system, or the best-funded users step off the shared network. Everyone else is then left on a grid that’s stretched, expensive and vulnerable.

During the coalition government when Letwin was in the Cabinet Office, we spent days worrying away at grid resilience.

As always, problems come home to roost in the centre of government whereas departments tend to work left to right. They push their agenda and it’s someone else’s job to worry about the broader consequences even when they come back to bite them.

In this case, the issue has been the Energy Department prioritising decarbonising power supply, although with Drax emitting more than 14 million tonnes of CO2 last year, it’s at least arguable that burning wood pellets isn’t such a green dream.

When I worked with Letwin it seemed easier for ministers to carve out time to worry about the long term and what might happen.

There is lots of chat inside Westminster about rewiring the state. But the actual wiring also needs a bit of attention.

The French supermarkets lost their yoghurt. If Britain gets this wrong, we lose the lights. And, as Letwin warned, we may struggle to turn them back on.

data.title: Guinness boom threatened by rival stout makers
data.description:
Guinness sales have fallen after cheaper rival stouts undercut its dominance of British pubs.

Owner Diageo, which also makes Johnnie Walker and Smirnoff, said sales in the UK and Ireland had fallen by “low single-digits” between July and September because of “unusually hotter weather and competitive pressure”.

Sir Dave Lewis, its chief executive, admitted that rival stouts were increasingly challenging Guinness in pubs and supermarkets.

He said: “Success draws competition. Guinness has been very successful. The competition is within stout.

“There’s some work for us to do there. Not rocket science but we need to do it.”

He also said the record-breaking heatwave this summer was a factor.

“We’ve had a very warm summer so the stout market does have some impact,” he added.

The slowdown marks a surprise reversal for Guinness, which has enjoyed a boom as younger drinkers flock to the beer thanks to its popularity on social media.

A pub challenge known as “splitting the G”, where drinkers use their first sip to try to get the head of the pint to align with the Guinness logo, has attracted increasing numbers of young people to the drink.

Rival brewers have sought to capitalise on the stout boom by tapping into the trend and offering cheaper alternatives.

Murphy’s Irish Stout, made by Heineken, recently struck a deal with Wetherspoons to be stocked across nearly 800 pubs, charging an average of £2.99 a pint compared with £3.80 for Guinness.

Beamish, also owned by Heineken, recently expanded in the UK after striking a distribution deal with a major pub supplier.

Guinness copycats have also emerged from the big breweries including Caffrey’s Black Stout, made by Molson Coors, as well as Tennent’s Stout and Jeremy Clarkson’s Hawkstone Black.

Diageo was forced to ration Guinness supplies to some British pubs two years ago. The stout’s share of beer sales in British pubs almost doubled from 9.3pc in 2022 to 17.5pc in March 2025, according to company figures.

Guinness’s dominance has historically given Diageo considerable pricing power, with publicans reluctant to stop stocking a drink that customers specifically demand.

However, landlords have repeatedly complained about its wholesale cost, which Diageo increased by another 5.2pc in April.

Cheaper rivals threaten that advantage by offering landlords potentially better margins.

Sir Dave, who took charge in January to revive the company’s fortunes, suggested Diageo could make targeted adjustments to remain competitive, although he ruled out sweeping price cuts.

He said: “We’re not talking about a dramatic repositioning here. We’re talking about precision, portfolio-specific work.”

However, he insisted Guinness had not lost market share in Britain or Ireland, arguing that the unusually warm weather had weakened demand for stout overall.

He also said there would be no repeat of the Guinness shortages that affected British pubs before Christmas two years ago.

Despite the slowdown, Guinness continued to record strong sales growth internationally, including in the US, Africa and parts of Europe.

Its American performance has been a rare bright spot for Diageo, whose spirits business has struggled amid weakening demand for premium drinks.

North American sales fell 3.6pc in the three months to September, with Don Julio and Casamigos tequila and Crown Royal whisky all recording double-digit declines.

Diageo’s total sales rose 1.2pc to $4.93bn (£3.75bn), beating analysts’ expectations.

Sir Dave is approaching his first anniversary in the job after launching a restructuring programme targeting $1bn in annual savings.

Diageo’s workforce shrank by almost 2,000 in the year to June.

data.title: Burnham to halt wind and solar subsidies in net zero climbdown
data.description:
Andy Burnham has ordered a halt to new wind and solar power subsidies in a net zero climbdown aimed at cutting household energy bills.

The Government revealed on Tuesday that next year’s auction of contracts for difference (CfDs) – a form of state support for renewable energy projects – will be paused to ensure it benefits consumers.

This year’s auction, known as auction round eight, is expected to continue as normal in the coming weeks. It is expected to award subsidies that could be worth hundreds of millions of pounds a year, paid for by households and businesses.

But Michael Shanks, the energy minister, told the House of Lords environment committee that next year’s auction was being put on hold so that the CfD programme could be reformed.

It follows concerns that the development of renewable power capacity is moving faster than work to upgrade the electricity grid.

This has resulted in network bottlenecks and vast amounts of power going to waste. It has also led to wind farms being paid hundreds of millions of pounds to switch off, a practice known as “curtailment”.

Mr Shanks told peers that the Government was drawing up a new plan to prevent too much future capacity being built in Scotland, which is behind the biggest bottlenecks. He said the way subsidies are awarded will also change.

CfDs are the UK’s flagship mechanism for supporting renewable energy projects and are ultimately funded through consumer bills.

They ensure generators are always paid a fixed strike price for the electricity they produce, regardless of market prices.

Developers win CfDs by putting forward projects and bidding for fixed prices in auctions, helping to ensure the strike prices are competitive.

Last year’s estimated CfD budget was £1.7bn, covering wind farms, solar farms and other clean technologies.

“The CfD process has been incredibly useful to give investors certainty to build new projects,” Mr Shanks said. But he added that “we do now want to pause” before the next auction round to “look at whether we need some more significant changes to the contracts for difference scheme to make sure they work for the consumers of the country”.

John Healey, the Chancellor, declared in last week’s Budget that Labour’s priority was “first and foremost cheaper energy”.

Whitehall sources told The Telegraph that his remarks signalled a demotion of the 2030 clean power targets championed by Ed Miliband, the Foreign Secretary, when he ran the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.

Dan Tomlinson, a Treasury minister, said after the Budget that Mr Burnham would pursue “a new energy pathway” to “bring energy costs down to help British business to compete and British households to cope”.

Pointing to the rising cost of wasted wind power, Mr Tomlinson said: “With growing constraint and distribution costs, it’s right that the system costs of all new power are considered.”

He added that the UK would “only procure clean power” through auction round eight “if we are confident it will lower bills” and “we will reform the contract for difference [for the next auction] to support building the lowest cost system, fixing market distortions and siting assets in the right place”.

Ministers have also imposed a moratorium on new levies and policy costs being added to bills.

The Government insists that it stands by the 2030 clean power targets, which aim to ensure that 95pc of electricity generated by the end of the decade comes from “clean” sources such as renewables, nuclear or batteries.

However, ministers have sought to downplay the commitment.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, told MPs last month that it would be “pretty hard” to deliver clean power while keeping bills down, having previously said that affordability was her top concern.

She also told a conference that while her department would “play its part” to try and reach Mr Miliband’s target, “the public doesn’t measure the success of our energy system in gigawatts – they measure it in bills”.

James Alexander, chief executive of the UK Sustainable Investment and Finance Association, which represents pension funds and other big financial backers, said: “Investors will be deeply concerned by comments from the energy minister today that cast doubt on next year’s renewable energy auction.”

He added: “The Contracts for Difference model has been a crucial driver of investment in clean power, helping to secure record offshore wind capacity this year and build a world-leading renewables sector.

“But telling markets the Government intends to review this process risks sending a worrying signal about the strength of the UK’s commitment to the energy transition.

“We now need to see urgent clarity on the future of this process, or the Government could put billions of pounds of capital at risk.”

The Government has been approached for comment.

data.title: Towering wall that blocked homeowner’s sea view removed
data.description:
A 16ft wall that blocked a homeowner’s sea view has been removed after a 14-month row.

Liz Bates said the value of her home in Bournemouth, Dorset, fell by an estimated £50,000 because the wall obstructed her view.

The wall screened a rooftop terrace on a flat being built in a neighbouring block but it did not have planning permission.

Planning inspectors ruled three months ago that it had a “harmful overbearing impact” on Mrs Bates’s home and the size of the roof terrace “far exceeded what could be reasonably described as modest”.

However, instead of admitting defeat and demolishing the wall, Eddie Fitzsimmons, the developer, submitted an application to replace the brick wall with an opaque glass screen.

Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole (BCP) council rejected the plans.

Builders have taken down the wall – which was erected in September 2025 – leaving temporary scaffolding in its place.

Mrs Bates said: “I want to say I’m really happy, but I fear they will still come back in a couple of months [with another application].”

The 43-year-old is one of about 100 residents who have claimed their lives have been “ruined” by the development of four cliff-top apartment blocks of 27 flats in front of their homes in the affluent Southbourne area of Bournemouth.

Mrs Bates argued the roof terrace would be big enough to stage large outdoor parties and the screen would do nothing to stop noise and smells drifting into her house.

In its latest application, Mr Fitzsimmons’ Vivir Estates company said the shortened roof terrace would not be big enough to host parties, and the glass screen would “not result in an overbearing impact” upon Mrs Bates’s home.

Chris Miell, of Pure Town Planning, who represented the developer, told the council’s planning committee: “The inspector’s decision specified the roof terrace as it was previously proposed. It doesn’t mean that any roof terrace is unacceptable at this site.

“It would not cause material harm to the living conditions of neighbouring properties and overcomes the planning inspector’s concerns.”

The two and four-storey blocks in the main development are being built on a former council car park in front of 24 existing properties.

BCP council put the Southbourne Crossroads car park site up for sale in 2017 when it was underused, and denied two planning applications for the site.

The local authority was overruled after an appeal from Vivir Estates.

data.title: The corporate raider at the centre of Poundland’s woes
data.description:
Mark Newton-Jones is the corporate raider at the centre of the Poundland controversy, which was branded by one Labour MP on Tuesday as an act of “predatory capitalism”.

The European chief of Gordon Brothers, the investment firm accused of unjustifiably trying to push the chain into administration, has his fingerprints all over the scene. He is the senior of a trio of Gordon Brothers men who sit on the board of Poundland’s parent company.

With a starring role in what has quickly made him a target for politicians across the spectrum, Newton-Jones has been forced to defend Gordon Brothers’ stewardship of the chain to the Government.

In a letter to David Bickerton, a Department for Business official, Newton-Jones said Gordon Brothers had put “significant working capital at risk” on Poundland. He also pointed to a series of factors including inflation, higher staffing costs and “severe levels of shoplifting” for its slide towards – though not yet into – insolvency.

MPs, though, were unmoved at Gordon Brothers’ attempts to downplay its part. Gareth Snell, the Labour MP for Stoke-on-Trent Central, said the distressed investor was guilty of “predatory capitalism”.

He is among a growing group of politicians, including Reform’s Robert Jenrick and Richard Tice, who allege that Gordon Brothers may have unnecessarily pushed Poundland to the brink in a cynical ploy to maximise its returns.

Hannah Spencer, the Green MP for Gorton and Denton, said it was another example of “private equity vultures who swoop in and prey on our high-street brands”.

Few foresaw the brickbats when Newton-Jones celebrated Gordon Brothers’ takeover of Poundland last summer for a token £1.

“We are delighted to provide Barry Williams [Poundland’s chief executive] and his management team with the financing to support the substantial turnaround of this iconic retailer,” he said at the time.

“We believe Poundland is an essential retailer serving UK consumers and plays an important role on the high street.”

Yet now tens of thousands of jobs are claimed to be at risk at Poundland, and in its supply chain. Gordon Brothers provided some fresh capital, but not enough to deliver on Newton-Jones’s bullish rhetoric.

Alix Partners, the consulting firm on stand-by to handle Poundland’s administration if last-ditch rescue talks fail, was quickly installed to oversee day-to-day cash management, or “count every penny” as one adviser described it.

By Christmas, Poundland’s management team was complaining privately that the business wasn’t receiving the funds it had been promised by Newton-Jones’s team.

According to a flattering profile on Gordon Brothers’ website, he has more than 35 years of experience “leading, operating and restructuring physical and digital retail brands”.

Yet the 59-year-old is no stranger to corporate car crashes, having been at the wheel when Mothercare spun off track six years ago.

Meanwhile, his skills include “strategy, marketing, design and buying, warehousing and distribution and property and investment”.

However, a source involved in the frantic attempts to save Poundland, said there was little evidence to suggest it had benefited from Newton-Jones’s purported retail nous.

“I’ve seen nothing to confirm he sat next to Barry [Williams] and said ‘This is what you should do,’ or asked anything much more than ‘What’s your plan?’ and ‘Can we see your numbers?’. This was the Barry and Shaun [Wills – Poundland’s finance director] show,” the person said.

The ‘Boomerang Boss’

In the world of corporate restructuring, an industry known for its swashbuckling ways, Newton-Jones is a divisive character.

A source who has sat across the table from him during the recent negotiations at Poundland described him as “pompous”. Despite this, away from work, Newton-Jones is said to be fond of a night out.

His record at Mothercare is equally up for debate. After being fired and rehired to run the ailing chain in the space of just a few weeks, he was given the nickname the “Boomerang Boss”.

The boardroom farce in 2018 saw him sacked minutes before his successor was announced to the stock market. Alan Parker, the chairman of Mothercare, told the City the board had “looked at the results over the last few years” and “unanimously decided to replace him”.

Yet just 36 days later, Parker was out and Newton-Jones was back after what he called a “forced sabbatical”.

But it wasn’t a happy return. Despite a brutal overhaul that included swathes of store closures, along with rent cuts, a multimillion-pound rights issue and debt refinancing, the disposal of its Early Learning Centre offshoot and a sale and leaseback of its Watford head office, Mothercare’s decline continued.

A mere 18 months after Mr Newton-Jones’s reappointment, Mothercare collapsed into administration.

Although insolvency laws required Poundland’s management to put administrators on standby, insiders are under no illusions about where the blame ultimately lies for its predicament.

“It takes a certain type of person to make thousands of people jobless just before Christmas,” someone on the other side of the negotiating table said of Newton-Jones.

No doubt, the vast majority of them will be hoping there’s no comeback for the Boomerang Boss this time.

data.title: Ex-Adidas boss sues builder after being told to partly demolish £1.3m home
data.description:
A former Adidas boss who was ordered to demolish part of his £1.3m home because it is two metres too long is suing the developer who sold it to him.

Edward Nixon, a former managing director of Adidas in Korea, and his wife, Sally, bought West Barn in East Haddon, Northamptonshire, and commissioned Barry Howard to convert it into a home.

Mr Howard, the head of Barry Howard Homes, a Northampton-based development company, sold the couple the £600,000 parcel of land on which West Barn stands and had already built a “shell of a house” on the site.

He struck a £700,000 deal with the couple to “finalise the construction of the house in accordance with drawings provided to the Nixons”.

The couple say they were told by Mr Howard during a video call in July 2020 that “the house is built and the planners are happy with it”.

But in June the following year, West Northamptonshire council imposed an enforcement notice, demanding that the Nixons either demolish their new home or carry out comprehensive alterations, telling them that the 36-metre barn conversion was two metres bigger than the approved plans.

The Nixons are now suing Mr Howard for £900,000 for “fraudulent misrepresentation” on the basis that he must have known the house was bigger than it should have been.

However, the developer is disputing the couple’s claim, insisting he had no idea the barn’s dimensions had gone over the limit when he sold it.

Daria Gleyze, the couple’s barrister, claimed at Central London county court that Mr Howard made a series of misleading statements which induced her clients to go ahead with buying into the conversion project, including the video call in July 2020.

And in September that year when filling out the standard inquiries form questionnaire accompanying the sale contract, Mr Howard answered “no” to the question, “are you aware of any breach of planning law in relation to the construction, use or occupation of the property”, the barrister said.

Ms Gleyze told Judge Nigel Gerald that the council demanded drastic alterations because of “its sheer bulk and mass deviating from the character and form of the original approved building”.

The court heard that the house also exceeded its permitted ridge height, where two opposing sloping roof planes meet, by just under one metre.

The local authority decided that the changes had “detracted from the character and appearance” of the original barn, and in December 2020, three months after completing the barn’s purchase, the Nixons discovered that the planning rules had been broken.

In June 2021, the council imposed an enforcement notice and the following year approved “remedial works” that would result in a “significant decrease in size and a different layout of the house”, Ms Gleyze explained.

“Their new house will have to be much smaller,” she told Judge Gerald.

Representing himself in court, Mr Howard insisted that he “had no knowledge that this building was being built in breach”, and claimed that Mr Nixon was “involved in every detail of the building’s design”.

Ms Gleyze called his defence “demonstrably untrue”, arguing: “It is inconceivable, and wholly fanciful to assert, that Mr Howard, who prides himself on being a professional builder with ample experience of building houses, would not have realised that he had deviated from the plans approved when he constructed the house, especially given the very significant discrepancies between the house as built and as approved.

“It is clear that the claimants suffered loss as a result of these misrepresentations. They were forced to incur significant costs in attempting to remedy the breach of planning and they will end up with a property significantly smaller and less valuable than what they had purchased.

“A valuation dated Oct 13, 2025, estimated a difference of £350,000 between the value of the house as built and as it would be after remedial planning measures are implemented.”

During a court hearing last week, Judge Gerald was asked to order “summary judgment” against Mr Howard on the grounds that he had “no realistic prospect” of defeating the claim against him.

But after a brief hearing, the judge agreed to Mr Howard’s request to have the case adjourned in order for him to gather more evidence and instruct solicitors.

“It seems fair to give Mr Howard a relatively brief opportunity to find new solicitors and put in a witness statement,” he said.

“The essence of his witness statement would be to explain why he didn’t know at the time that the representation which was made was wrong.”

The judge also noted evidence produced by the Nixons from the project’s architect “on one reading to the effect that prior to Sept 22 Mr Howard had been told that the planning regulations had been breached”.

The judge adjourned the case until late November.

data.title: Landlords on the hook for renters’ energy debts under government plans
data.description:
Landlords could be on the hook for their tenants’ energy bills under government plans to stop people moving home without settling their debts.

New proposals from watchdog Ofgem, published to coincide with the Budget on Wednesday, would make landlords legally responsible for ensuring energy companies know the identity of renters so they can target individuals directly with bills.

If property owners fail to provide accurate details, they risk becoming responsible for any gas and electricity bills run up by their tenants.

It follows research showing that up to 40pc of the estimated £6bn in domestic energy debts has been run up by defaulting tenants who skip between properties, leaving unpaid bills.

Total debt could rise to £11bn in the coming years, Ofgem has warned.

Ofgem’s consultation said: “Government will introduce legislation to Parliament to reform the home moves process, placing a new obligation on landlords to provide timely and accurate information to their supplier when tenants move into or out of a property.

“Where neither the tenant nor landlord has provided the necessary information, landlords may become liable for energy charges associated with the property … The reform would place similar obligations on landlords as exist with respect of water bills in England and Wales.”

The proposals sparked an immediate backlash from the property industry.

Timothy Douglas, the head of policy at Propertymark, the professional body for estate agents, said: “There is a need to prevent energy debt accumulating when tenants move in or out ... 

“But we do not agree with the proposal that landlords may become liable for energy charges when it is tenants that have used and accumulated the debt.”

The move follows growing concern about the apparently inexorable rise in domestic energy debts, especially since the energy crises caused first by the Ukraine conflict and now by Donald Trump’s attack on Iran.

In 2020, before the conflicts, debts totalled about £1bn, but the subsequent surge in prices hit household budgets hard, leaving many unable to pay.

This prompted energy suppliers to accelerate the installation of prepayment meters, with nearly 100,000 homes forcibly switched under court warrants, while many others had smart meters remotely set to prepay mode.

In 2023 Charities such as Citizens Advice reported record-breaking numbers of consumers who were “self-disconnecting” – left without heat or electricity in the depths of winter because they could not afford to top up their meters.

That was followed by revelations that British Gas debt collectors executing court warrants had forcibly entered homes to install prepayment meters, including those of vulnerable customers.

The Government immediately banned such measures. But that in turn saw energy debts accelerate to around £6bn now.

Ofgem also found that while many households were unable to pay, many others, mainly renters, were able but unwilling.

Debts to be forgiven

John Healey on Wednesday announced a £100 payment for all homes in council tax bands A-D, plus a debt write-off scheme targeted at bill payers receiving means-tested benefits, disability benefits, or pension credit who have accumulated energy arrears since 2022.

Under the scheme, their debts will be forgiven with the cost “socialised”, meaning it will be added to general energy bills.

This could cost around £5 a year – but comes on top of the £67 already added to bills to cover longer-term customer debts.

Energy industry figures say Labour’s latest measures will do little to resolve the problem of surging debt.

Prashant Kachhala, from energy consultancy Baringa, said: “One-off payments and tariff changes may slow new arrears, but they do not address the stock of debt already concentrated among households with no realistic ability to repay.

“That unpaid debt is ultimately spread across every bill payer, so without structural change the cost of doing nothing keeps rising.”

The consultation is also backed by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.

data.title: Lime riders joust as knights in London
data.description:
Lime bike riders have been filmed dressed as knights and duelling in London.

The company has said its bikes are “not for jousting” after videos circulated on social media showed hundreds of people gathered in London Fields, east London, to watch Saturday’s event.

Artist Jack Carden and actor Cameron Carnegie-Brown, known as Camtholomew, were filmed jousting whilst riding the green rentable e-bikes.

Dressed in chainmail, red and black cloaks and armour, including helmets, the pair ride towards one another, brandishing striped poles.

The assembled crowd can be heard chanting “joust, joust, joust” before one of the men strikes the other with a “lance”, causing them to fall from the bike.

A spokesman for Lime said on Monday: “We always love seeing Londoners come together and build a sense of community in unexpected ways.

“While we appreciate the medieval spirit, safety must always come first.

“Lime bikes are designed for getting around the city, not for jousting.

“We discourage anyone from attempting similar events, to help keep riders and those around them safe.”

Posting on social media before the event, Mr Carden said the “free public joust” was “performance art”.

In a video from the event posted to both competitors’ social media accounts, a voiceover says: “I want to remind you all why we are here. 

“Not only does this mean some artistic violence but to come together and celebrate art, to remind ourselves that we’re all the same and that what we need right now in this world is a little bit more love.”

A video on Mr Carden’s Instagram account of the joust has been watched more than four million times.

data.title: Labour gives railway trade union activists a ‘blank cheque’
data.description:
Labour has been accused of giving rail union activists a “blank cheque” to campaign during work hours.

Groups including the RMT, the Transport Salaried Staffs’ Association and the Aslef train drivers’ association will be allowed to carry out trade union work while being paid as if they were in their day jobs.

Keir Mather, a junior minister, said that the Department for Transport (DfT)’s passenger train agency, DfT Operator, had signed a “voluntary recognition agreement” with the three main rail unions.

That agreement, the minister said, had no limits on taxpayer funding of trade union activism during normal working hours. The funding will be supplied via Great British Railways, the planned state body unifying the rail network.

Richard Holden MP, the shadow transport secretary, said: “It’s crystal clear that Andy Burnham’s Labour Government is repeating Keir Starmer’s mistakes and giving a blank cheque to their trades union paymasters on the trains – this time with so called ‘facility time’ which, in reality, means political campaigning at the expense of passengers and taxpayers.

“Rather than raising taxes and fares to pay for union activity, the Government should be concentrating on making railways cheaper, safer and more reliable for passengers and taxpayers,” the Conservative MP added.

“Sadly under Labour, serving the unions rather than the public will always be their top priority.”

Union sources say that facility time consists of up to 50 per cent of a worker’s normal contracted hours which can be spent performing activities such as identifying health and safety problems or dealing with workplace disciplinary problems.

This is claimed to save employers money by avoiding the need to hire more HR staff.

Previously, under the Civil Service’s wider Facility Time Framework document, government departments were not allowed to spend more than 0.1 per cent of their annual salary bill on trade union activists’ facility time.

This would have limited DfT and its agencies, such as DfT Operator or the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, to a maximum of about £58,000 per year being spent on facility time.

But Mr Mather confirmed that all limits have been lifted. In a parliamentary response to a question posed by Mr Holden, he said: “The [trade union] agreement does not prescribe a fixed facility time entitlement, budget or payroll percentage.

“Instead, reasonable paid time off for accredited representatives will be managed in line with legislation, Acas guidance and operational requirements.

“As facility time will vary according to operational need and levels of trade union activity, it is not currently possible to provide a reliable estimate of its annual cost or proportion of payroll,” he added, saying that such paid time off “will be managed proportionately, balancing statutory obligations, operational delivery and value for money considerations”.

Facility time includes activities such as attending union conferences during working hours, as well as “union facing” projects such as branch meetings.

Critics have said Labour’s watering down of rules ensuring that public sector union members are not paid for non-work activities during work time effectively channels cash into the unions’ pockets.

Trade unions fund the Labour Party and individual Labour MPs to the tune of millions of pounds per year.

Key taxpayer protections against union misuse of facility time were torn up by Sir Keir Starmer’s government, including laws ensuring departments revealed how much facility time was granted to union activists.

Labour also weakened transparency laws around trade union financing, making it harder for the public to understand and scrutinise how much money unions are pouring into political donations, as well as identifying the sources and targets of that funding.

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “Any suggestion that these arrangements provide a blank cheque for facility time is wrong.

“The voluntary recognition agreement that DfT Operator has reached applies only to union representation for a small number of predominantly former DfT employees who transferred into DfT Operator and does not extend to the whole industry.

“We are taking a pragmatic approach that reflects established industrial relations practice and means workplace issues can be dealt with constructively.”

The spokesman also denied that the agreement applied to DFT Operator staff who were members of the RMT, TSSA or Aslef unions, without giving further detail.

data.title: Just 10pc of shoplifters responsible for 70pc of thefts
data.description:
Just 10 per cent of shoplifters are responsible for 70 per cent of store thefts in Britain, research has revealed.

The prolific offenders commit an average of 40 offences, as recorded by police, but are likely to be behind many more for which they are not caught, or for which they do not admit responsibility.

While more than 500,000 offences are recorded by police annually, the British Retail Consortium estimates there are some 5.5 million store thefts in a year, resulting in direct losses of £2.2bn.

That means the top 10 per cent of prolific offenders could be responsible for as many as 3.8 million thefts at a cost of £1.4bn a year.

The figures have been revealed by Auror, a company that provides police forces and retailers including Marks & Spencer, Tesco and Boots with a data-sharing system that enables them to identify prolific offenders.

‘Brazen, organised, aggressive’

Shops are able to submit CCTV footage, photos and evidence about all their repeat shoplifters to a database.

Auror, based in New Zealand, then provides police with the data they need to speed up investigations and target the 10 per cent who are prolific offenders.

Similar data analysed by the Met Police found 104 prolific shoplifters were responsible for 4,389 offences in the past two years, a third of all store thefts in London for which a suspect had been identified.

Retail chiefs say thieves have become “more brazen, more organised and more aggressive” amid a fourfold increase in shoplifting since the Covid pandemic. It has risen to record highs of more than 500,000 offences a year in England and Wales.

Thefts have, however, started to plateau, and data published by Auror show that violence by shoplifters in stores has fallen since police and shops started targeting prolific offenders.

High street shops in London and Manchester have experienced a 21 per cent and 20 per cent reduction respectively in the rate of violence this year compared with last year, according to the Auror data, which cover tens of thousands of shops in Britain.

Violent incidents were down 24 per cent overall in British shops, and have fallen by 22 per cent in Scotland and 32 per cent in Wales.

Among prolific offenders identified by retailers were a violent thief who stole £50,000 worth of products in Manchester, London and Norwich, and another violent shoplifter linked to more than 70 thefts or assaults in 19 stores around Glasgow.

Data system has ‘positive impact’

Roisin Currie, the chief executive of Greggs, said: “Retail crime remains a challenge for retailers across the UK, which is why we continue to invest in a range of measures to help keep our shops safe and welcoming places to work and visit.

“Through our use of Auror, alongside other security measures and close collaboration with police and industry partners, we’re improving how incidents are reported, helping to identify repeat offenders and supporting more effective action against those causing the greatest harm.

Mark Gleeson, Auror’s general manager for Britain and Europe, said: “Stores are able to make more informed decisions about risk and safety by focusing on the top offenders driving the majority of harm across retail, and using that intelligence to work more effectively with police.”

data.title: Elon Musk to kill off Tesla’s Cybertruck
data.description:
Elon Musk is to end production of Tesla’s Cybertruck after sales of the controversial electric pick-up proved a disappointment.

The electric carmaker’s chief executive signalled last night that production of the Cybertruck will wind down in 2027, making way for the business to produce more robotaxis at its Texas Gigafactory.

Posting on social media, Mr Musk said: “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

The announcement comes just three years after the Cybertruck first went on sale.

Mr Musk had hailed the three-ton vehicle as “bulletproof” and “apocalypse-proof”, while the company’s website promotes its “ultra-hard stainless-steel exoskeleton” and a range of up to 325 miles.

However, the truck’s high price dampened demand among motorists.

It was initially set to cost $39,999 (£30,600) but the cheapest version now starts at $60,000 (£45,900).

Tesla sold just 11,586 Cybertrucks in the first nine months of 2026, according to analysts Cox Automotive, far below Mr Musk’s previous predictions of 250,000 sales a year.

While Mr Musk had billed the pick-up as the ultimate off-road electric vehicle, the Cybertruck has suffered from a series of mishaps and faults before and after it went on sale.

When demonstrating the truck’s toughened glass during its 2019 launch event, a Tesla executive threw a ball bearing at its window, causing it to shatter.

Tesla has also been forced to issue recalls of the truck over braking issues and other problems, including the vehicle’s trim falling off.

Several trucks have been involved in accidents where they have burst into fireballs after a crash.

Mr Musk took the decision to end production as he attempts to revive Tesla by focusing on AI, robotics and driverless taxis, increasing production of its Cybercab vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots.

The company has launched ride-hailing services in a handful of US cities, while it is planning to build up to 125,000 autonomous electric cabs per year at its flagship Texas plant.

Shares in Mr Musk’s companies have plunged this week after the Democrats swung to victory in the US midterm elections, taking both the House and the Senate.

Tesla’s stock is down more than 12pc since Tuesday, while SpaceX is down 11pc. Mr Musk’s net worth plummeted by close to $80bn in one day on Thursday to around $785bn, according to Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index.
