data.title: How the Bank of England is strangling the economy
data.description:
Banks put on a brave face last week as they were subject to yet another windfall tax by the Government, this time to pay for emergency energy bills.

But tucked away in the Budget was a rare bit of good news. In a letter, John Healey, the Chancellor, signalled that the Treasury was prepared to back calls from industry to unpick a series of post-financial-crisis rules that banks say are holding back the economy.

In the note, Healey reflected the arguments bank bosses have long made: that a complex web of rules devised by the Bank of England are unfairly penalising British banks, strangling lending to households and businesses.

“It is crucial that our regulatory framework is internationally competitive, promotes competition and acts to support, rather than unduly constrain, investment in the UK economy,” Healey said.

Ever since the financial crisis, regulators have stuck to strict rules governing how banks can lend. These broadly focus on how much capital a bank must hold on its balance sheet against each loan it gives out, in case it defaults.

Some of these standards are set internationally but domestic regulators add their own requirements.

In the UK, the extra capital demands introduced by the Bank of England have been criticised as overly cautious, with the ultimate effect of making it harder for British banks to lend into the economy and penalising the City to the benefit of international rivals.

These criticisms have only sharpened as mortgage rates continue to climb, with an average five-year deal hitting 6pc in early October, the highest level in three years.

The war in Iran, higher inflation and energy costs and a world-wide sell-off in bond markets are the main culprits for rising mortgage rates – but banks argue that capital rules are not helping.

UK banks aren’t the only ones to complain about excessively restrictive post-crisis rules. The boss of UBS said last week that the lender was seriously considering leaving Switzerland in protest against a planned tightening of the same set of rules.

A lighter-touch regime could be to Britain’s benefit. During her time as chancellor Rachel Reeves reportedly pitched London as a potential new home for UBS in discussions with Colm Kelleher, the bank’s chairman.

Last December, the Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee relaxed some of the requirements for the first time since the financial crisis. With another review due later this year, lenders are hoping for a further reprieve.

“It’s fair to say that the measures announced to date have not had a terribly significant impact in terms of our ability to sponsor lending and indeed growth in the UK economy,” Will Chalmers, the chief financial officer of Lloyds Bank, said last week.

“We’ll see what the Financial Policy Committee comes out with [but] it comes back to a very similar point to around tax ... What we really want is just a stable and a predictable regulatory regime that in turn is conducive to growth.”

As the banks see it, nowhere are the rules more lopsided than around mortgages. Big lenders use their own financial models to determine how risky an individual mortgage is but these are then overseen by the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), the Bank of England body that regulates banks.

Concerned that the banks’ calculations weren’t up to scratch, the PRA set two extra requirements. Their models needed to factor in default rates from the early 1990s recession, as well as a 25pc fall in house prices.

House prices have never fallen by a quarter across the UK and mortgages look very different from the 1990s, which means that the models that British banks factor into their mortgage lending are far more conservative than international rules demand.

Banks argue this means they can’t give out as many mortgages as they would want to, pushing rates upwards.

Asked last week whether the PRA’s rules needed tweaking, Paul Thwaite, the boss of NatWest, said: “UK mortgages are a very obvious example... we need to make sure the levels of capital there genuinely reflect the risk and are proportionate.”

Healey’s concerns have focused on a separate issue – whether some of the bank rules overlap, with the ultimate effect being that UK banks and their lending are unfairly penalised.

The amount of capital that each bank has to hold is composed of a number of building blocks, each designed to guard against a particular risk.

Banks that are considered domestically important – such as Lloyds or NatWest – are required to hold more capital.

There is also a separate buffer that essentially acts as a “rainy day” fund.

This is to ensure that if there is an economic downturn, banks don’t respond to it by cutting lending and making the downturn worse.

However, these two buffers, and another one that penalises banks for having their lending concentrated in one area, broadly have the same effect: making it harder to lend to British businesses and provide mortgages.

Lending to small businesses, for instance, is still about a third lower than it was 15 years ago, according to the British Business Bank.

As the banks see it, these stringent rules have the strange effect that the capital requirements for NatWest or Lloyds are tougher than for some of the biggest banks in the world.

As of the first quarter of 2026, the capital ratio average across all UK banks stood at 15.1pc, while the equivalent ratio for JP Morgan and Goldman Sachs was just 14.3pc and 12.5pc respectively.

“The Bank of England is not perfect but it does have a pretty good reputation in terms of having reduced risk in the UK banking system post the 2008 financial crisis,” said Benjamin Toms, an analyst at RBC.

“When you compare bank capital versus US peers, UK requirements do look more onerous but it’s very difficult sometimes to see if you are comparing apples with apples.”

Banks are hopeful that the upcoming review by the Bank of England could loosen some of these overlapping requirements.

Yet for its part, the Bank of England has pushed back. In a report in July, it reaffirmed its position that capital requirements were broadly appropriate as they stand. The Bank declined to comment.

Major UK banks had seen a period of robust results with bumper dividends and share buybacks, the report said, which suggested that capital requirements weren’t a constraint on lending.

It also argued there was no simple way of comparing capital rules for US and UK banks.

However, the City is hopeful that the Bank of England might be more receptive this time after Katharine Braddick, a former executive at Barclays, took over the top job at the PRA in July.

“We don’t disagree that financial stability is important,” says Nala Worsfold, of UK Finance.

“We just think that it’s gone past the tipping point of endangering and adversely impacting growth. And the country needs growth.

“We are not talking about deregulation, we are just talking about maybe taking away some of the gold plating – some of the extra level of prudence.”

data.title: Apple cuts staff AI usage in scramble to rein in costs
data.description:
Apple has restricted employees’ use of AI in an effort to cut costs.

The tech giant – the world’s most valuable company – reduced engineering staff’s daily usage caps from $300 (£223) a day to $200, according to Bloomberg.

The company is reportedly considering further cuts to reduce the daily cap to $100 and slash non-technical staff’s budgets from $100 a day to $25.

It makes the company the latest to rein in employees’ use of AI, amid concerns about costs and questions about productivity.

Revolut, Britain’s most valuable tech start-up, said this week that it had saved substantial sums by moving staff from using expensive “frontier” systems to cheaper Chinese models running on its own servers.

Accenture last month stopped some staff from spending more than $29 a month on AI after employees racked up huge bills.

Uber and Tesla have also imposed cuts, while Microsoft and Meta have cut their use of Anthropic’s chatbot, Claude.

According to Bloomberg, Apple is pushing staff to use more AI to boost productivity, even as it imposes spending limits.

The financial limits apply to how many “tokens” – units of AI consumption – that employees require. More efficient and less powerful AI models typically use fewer tokens to carry out tasks.

Some companies have pushed employees to use cheaper models instead of using expensive systems by default.

The changes are among the first introduced by John Ternus, Apple’s new chief executive, who took over from Tim Cook in September. The company did not comment.

Employees at some companies briefly engaged in “tokenmaxxing” earlier this year, with staff encouraged to spend heavily on AI. But concerns about cost and productivity led to a swift reversal.

Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, has said that engineers should be spending an amount equal to half their annual salary on AI tokens.

The trend of cutting AI use has raised concerns about giant initial public offerings (IPOs) planned by Anthropic and OpenAI. Sales growth slowed at Anthropic in the third quarter of the year.

Investors have said the company may now go public at a valuation of $1.5tn or less, below earlier hopes for a $2tn valuation.

data.title: National Lottery operator overhauls senior team as ticket sales slump
data.description:
The operator of the National Lottery has overhauled its senior team as it scrambles to halt a drop in ticket sales.

Allwyn, which secured the licence in 2022, is parting ways with three of its top executives as part of a major restructuring.

Mark Smith, the chief technology officer, will leave the business but remain an adviser until June next year.

Sarah Venning, the chief strategy and transformation officer, and Richard Dawkins, the managing director of digital, will also step down in the coming weeks.

Phil Walker, a former managing director at William Hill, took over from Andria Vidler last month as chief executive.

The overhaul follows a series of technical problems and growing scrutiny of Allwyn’s stewardship of the National Lottery.

Richard Desmond, the former owner of the Daily Express and Channel 5, was defeated this year in a £1.3bn legal battle against the Gambling Commission concerning its decision not to award him the National Lottery licence.

Yet Allwyn, which is owned by Czech billionaire Karel Komárek, is under mounting pressure after its failure to deliver on pledges made during the bidding process.

The company promised to increase charitable donations from almost £18bn under its predecessor, Camelot, to £38bn, equivalent to £3.8bn a year in the coming decade.

But it later watered down this figure, pledging instead to double the amount it contributes to good causes from £30m to £60m a week, or almost £3.2bn a year.

Figures released this week by the Gambling Commission showed the National Lottery’s payments to charitable projects fell further in the latest quarter to £388.3m, down from £460.9m a year earlier.

The regulator said the decrease reflected lower sales “across all existing games”, with the sharpest falls in EuroMillions and Lotto.

Alongside its legal battle, Allwyn has been hampered by a botched digital transformation, including delays to a major upgrade of ageing IT systems.

The National Audit Office, the Government’s spending watchdog, last month opened an investigation into the design of the lottery licence amid concerns about the amount of money being distributed to good causes.

The Department for Culture, Media and Sport is carrying out a separate review of how money from lottery ticket sales is spent. The Telegraph also revealed that Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, is pushing to bring the National Lottery into public ownership.

Under the restructuring, the company will also create two new roles: a chief digital officer and a chief marketing officer.

Mr Walker said: “The transformation of the National Lottery has involved an enormous amount of work across our business.

“Our challenge now is to turn that transformation into stronger growth, a better experience for players and retail partners, and more money for good causes.

“That means putting customers closer to our decisions, giving our retail and digital businesses the capabilities they need to compete and innovate, and creating much clearer accountability for performance.”

data.title: Britain’s energy policy is driving us to Middle East, says gas storage boss
data.description:
The owner of one of Britain’s biggest gas-storage facilities is ditching investment in the UK for the Middle East because of the Government’s crippling energy policies, its chief executive said.

Peter Mann, head of energy group Kistos, said future spending by the company would go to places such as Oman because the UK lacked a stable tax regime for oil and gas.

He said the Middle East would remain more appealing than the UK until energy strategy was taken out of ministers’ hands and given to an independent regulatory body.

Mann said this would mean “people know where they stand”.

“That ultimately is the key to investment. That stability has gone in the UK,” he said.

Kistos Energy owns Hill Top, one of the few remaining gas storage sites in the UK that can deliver the gas equivalent of 11pc of the UK’s daily total.

The 46-year-old, son of colourful ex-army officer and mercenary Simon Mann, and, like his father, a former officer in the Scots Guards, founded the company just six years ago.

Since then it has followed a trajectory similar, albeit on a smaller scale, to that of Neo Next+, the 2018 start-up that is now the UK North Sea’s biggest operator.

Both have bought up assets pioneered by energy majors but then sold off as they quit the North Sea – driven out by the UK’s divisive energy politics.

Mann says he would like to invest more in the UK, including in gas storage projects like Hill Top, but is exasperated by the constant regulatory changes politicians have imposed on the oil and gas industry in recent years.

Kistos is still investing in the UK – but only just.

It has bought the nearby Hole House gas caverns too and plans to reopen them for gas storage in the next couple of years.

Mann thinks Kistos is the only UK company spending private capital to actually increase the country’s domestic gas storage capacity.

Back in 2022, it also bought into gas production with stakes in four fields off the Shetlands known as the Greater Laggan area, along with associated pipelines and a gas plant.

But frustrated by an unpredictable windfall tax regime, bureaucratic paralysis over North Sea drilling and a political class that treats energy policy as a tactical football, Kistos’s future investments are mostly heading abroad.

It has recently spent $148m (£110m) on stakes in oil fields in Oman, with plans to invest a further $100m in the next three years, plus similar amounts in Norway’s North Sea – where Kistos bought Mime Petroleum in 2023.

“I think we are the only ones in the UK investing in increasing the capacity of gas storage at this point in time ... But Kistos is not in a place where it has to do things just in the UK, so we can be selective and opportunistic in where we see value,” he says.

Such views are increasingly common in the UK oil and gas sector.

For Britain, the consequences of this domestic investment freeze are severe – the decline of the North Sea and the UK’s inadequate storage means the country haemorrhages billions each year.

That goes on importing foreign energy – especially gas – subsidising overseas jobs and tax revenues while exposing British households to extreme winter volatility.

If Britain manages to keep the lights on and avoid gas shortages this coming winter, it will be thanks in no small part to some of the nation’s largest but least visible assets which are owned by Kistos.

They lie deep beneath the rolling fields of Cheshire comprising an array of giant salt caverns pumped full of pressurised natural gas which are now amongst our most vital gas supply bulwarks.

Cheshire’s salt caverns are among the UK’s least appreciated geological assets. Around 200 million years ago the region was covered in shallow seas that evaporated, leaving salt layers hundreds of metres thick, now buried deep underground.

They have been mined for centuries – providing, for example, the rock salt that keeps our roads free of ice.

But it’s the impermeable caverns drilled into the remaining salt, 600 metres below ground, that are now filled with gas, the region’s most vital energy asset.

“Our caverns are connected to the national transmission network,” said Mann. “We can empty them really quickly and do 11pc of [the] UK’s daily gas requirement, but then you can fill it up quite quickly in three or four days and do the same thing again.”

That facility means companies like Kistos can respond fast to changes in demand for gas – releasing more if temperatures plunge and demand surges. Or soaking up surpluses when demand falls.

That buffers the UK’s gas consumers against shortages. And it’s also profitable – for example by exploiting price swings to buy when demand falls or supply surges, and then reselling as prices go up.

It sounds like an easy way to make money, but Kistos is now one of just a handful of companies still operating in this market.

Its nearest rival is Storengy, a subsidiary of French energy giant Engie, which runs the nearby Stublach site.

Another used to be Centrica, owners of British Gas and of the much larger Rough gas storage site – a depleted gas field in the North Sea that could hold about three weeks’ worth of UK gas supply.

However, Chris O’Shea, the Centrica boss, has declared that the site cannot run at a profit and plans to shut it down next April – unless the Government provides funding.

The caverns under Cheshire that now help underpin UK gas supplies could have gone the same way.

Another facility at Hatfield Moor, near Doncaster, shut down two decades ago, while EDF shut down the Hole House site, in Cheshire, just a few years ago. Hole House is now being reopened by Kistos.

Those closures are one reason why the UK is facing this winter with a wafer-thin margin of gas reserves. “We now have just six or seven days of security of storage available in the UK,” warns Mann.

His warnings are echoed by many others.

UK storage is only 36pc full, according to energy economist Nick Butler, a former BP vice-president and Downing Street adviser.

“That is well below the level in other countries across Europe ... In the circumstances, it is surprising that the UK Energy Secretary has not made a statement on the issue to Parliament,” he wrote on Substack.

Until the UK restores commercial sanity to its energy policy, Cheshire’s salt caverns will remain an isolated buffer against the cold while British capital investment continues to find a warmer, more welcoming home under the desert sun.

data.title: Burnham to make new North Sea drilling illegal
data.description:
Andy Burnham is poised to ban drilling for new oil and gas in the UK to end exploration in the North Sea.

The Prime Minister has backed an energy bill that would put into law a permanent prohibition on new drilling, a move to make it harder for ministers to reverse the ban in future.

Energy exploration in the UK is subject to the temporary moratorium originally imposed by Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary, but this could be lifted by a future energy secretary.

Mr Burnham is now supporting new laws being introduced by Mr Miliband’s successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh, that would make it harder to reopen the North Sea.

Repealing the proposed new law would need a parliamentary majority.

The Government said the energy independence bill would deliver on its “pragmatic approach to the North Sea, by ending new licences to explore new oil and gas fields while supporting continued production from existing licensed areas”.

If approved by Parliament, the new laws would allow oil companies to keep operating existing licensed oil and gas fields until they are depleted.

But they would be able to drill new wells only if they could be connected to existing infrastructure by subsea pipelines known as tiebacks.

The move follows the approval last month of the Jackdaw gas field, which operates under an existing licence and uses a tieback to pump gas into established pipelines.

Labour is yet to make a decision on the giant Rosebank oil field, west of Shetland, which also has an existing licence.

Both the Conservatives and Reform UK have pledged to restart North Sea exploration and drilling were they to win power.

Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, criticised Mr Burnham’s plans warning: “Labour’s so-called energy independence bill will only make Britain more dependent on oil and gas imports. Labour might as well hang a ‘closed for business’ sign over our North Sea.”

The legislation honours Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledge, which stated: “We will not issue new licences to explore new fields because they will not take a penny off bills, cannot make us energy secure and will only accelerate the worsening climate crisis. In addition, we will not grant new coal licences and will ban fracking for good.”

Some energy insiders and investors disagree, including Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos group.

David Bucknall, the head of subsidiary Ineos Energy, which has a raft of North Sea assets, said: “The Government’s legislation to ban new drilling in the North Sea would actively decrease energy security in the UK.

“Leaving existing resources in the ground at home while we import the same resources from abroad makes our energy autonomy a victim of global instability.”

Analyst Ashley Kelty, from Panmure Liberum, said: “This bill just highlights the lunacy of net zero dogma.

“It’s risible that they try to say that it’s pragmatic to stop the UK producing more oil and gas. It’s clearly a reaction to poor polling against the Greens. I see this as more vibe driven policy making as opposed to ‘pragmatic’ policy making.”

Dan Slater, from Zeus Capital, said: “While banning new exploration licences via legislation makes resumption a more circuitous process, the logic for new licences is inescapable, and parliament is sovereign and fully has the power to reverse the new ban.”

David Whitehouse, the chief executive of Offshore Energies UK, a trade body for Britain’s oil and gas producers, said the planned bill would simply make the UK more dependent on imported oil and gas.

“This will leave households and businesses exposed in an increasingly volatile world. We should be making the most of the energy we produce here at home rather than relying on imports.”

data.title: China blamed for loss of half a million German factory jobs
data.description:
China has been blamed for the loss of half a million German factory jobs since 2019, as experts have warned that Europe’s manufacturing engine is losing momentum.

German industry shed 496,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute in Dresden, representing a drop of 7.1pc.

Joachim Ragnitz, the managing director at Ifo Dresden, said: “Employment is shrinking in almost all industrial sectors, which is likely a result of declining competitiveness, particularly vis-à-vis China.

“Traditional German core sectors, such as the automotive industry and mechanical engineering, are particularly hard hit.”

The figures follow warnings of a “China shock 2.0” as the world’s second-largest economy pumps out cheap advanced-manufacturing exports that threaten to crush Western industry. China’s trade surplus with Germany has doubled in the last year.

It brings back painful memories of the first shock in the early 2000s, when China unleashed a wave of cheap toys, clothes and manufactured goods into Western economies.

In addition to growing competition from China, the Ifo Institute also blamed vanishing factory jobs on a fresh wave of de-industrialisation triggered by high energy prices and changing demographics.

Europe’s biggest economy has suffered several shocks in recent years, reeling in particular from losing access to cheap Russian gas after the Ukraine war.

As factory jobs have disappeared, hiring in less productive sectors has risen significantly.

The services sector employs 2.2 million more people than in 2019, mainly in health and social care and public administration.

Mr Ragnitz warned that this would spell trouble for the future, as these jobs were unlikely to provide a significant boost to growth.

He said: “The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future.”

Car manufacturers and their suppliers have cut 123,500 jobs since 2019, a plunge of 13pc. Meanwhile, metal products manufacturers cut 115,600 jobs, and mechanical engineering another 64,500.

These three sectors account for 60pc of the job losses.

By contrast, service providers saw strong growth with 391,000 new jobs in healthcare and 357,000 in social services, including nursing homes.

Mr Ragnitz said the country’s ageing population was the key driver of this trend.

Germany has for years had a relatively low fertility rate. It improved briefly for a few years before and during Covid, before plunging again to its current level of 1.3 children per woman.

A fierce backlash against immigration means politicians may struggle to offset such demographic pressures.

Industrial decline has caused job losses in every part of Germany apart from Hamburg. Jobs are also falling faster in the east than in the west, at 8.4pc vs 6.8pc. In Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt, overall employment has even declined.

These are both states where the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is popular, with the hard-Right party winning the largest vote share in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt last month. It also won the state election in Thuringia in 2024.

data.title: Russia denies hacking supermarket fridges
data.description:
Russia has denied involvement in a hacking spree targeting supermarket fridges across Europe.

Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesman, said it was “absurd” to suggest that Russian-backed hackers were behind the assault, saying there were “no arguments or evidence” to support the claim.

Cyber security experts are scrambling to identify the hackers who launched a string of attacks on supermarket fridges and freezers, remotely turning up the temperatures to make the food inside unsafe to eat.

The cyber criminals targeted supermarkets across France last month and stores in Belgium, Sweden and Finland this week, leading to millions of euros worth of losses.

France’s blood bank was also hacked, while in the UK a handful of food suppliers have reported that their fridge units had their temperatures turned up to dangerous levels.

On Wednesday, two pro-Russian “hacktivist” groups, dubbed NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest, took credit for the attacks in posts on the encrypted messaging app Telegram.

However, Mr Peskov said the claims were “unfounded accusations against our country”.

The hackers exploited weaknesses in the systems that connect industrial refrigerators to the internet, taking them over remotely and tampering with them.

Some cyber security researchers have suggested the attacks bear the hallmarks of Russia as they hunt for a culprit.

However, other experts cast doubt on the groups’ claims, arguing the hackers – who are also known as the Cyber Army of Russia Reborn – are typically responsible for more opportunistic attacks.

Oleg Shakirov, an expert on Russian cyber activity, said: “Their claim doesn’t look plausible to me.”

UK security officials have yet to blame any one group for the hack and believe it is too early to identify those behind the incidents with any certainty.

However, other cyber investigators said they were exploring potential Russian links.

Xavier Bellekens, founder of the cyber security company Lupovis, said it had set up decoy internet signals designed to look like vulnerable fridge units.

He said hackers tried to target these. The attackers’ internet traffic included signals originating in Russia.

“It could be North Korea making a false flag,” he said, “but there are many little breadcrumbs that make us point to Russia.”

He added: “If it quacks like a duck and walks like a duck...”

Last month’s hacks in France affected fridges supplied by Danish cooling giant Danfoss. Danfoss said the machines had been running outdated software.

Other hacks have hit cooling technology systems developed by US business Copeland. Copeland has urged customers to update their software.

A spokesman for NHS Blood and Transport said it was undertaking “additional checks as an extra precaution” to secure its fridges following the attacks.

A spokesman for the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said: “We are aware of a small number of UK organisations that may be affected by this incident as a result of vulnerabilities on their systems, and the NCSC is supporting those that may be impacted.

“We continue to liaise with our international partners and the affected sectors to understand and mitigate its impact, and as you would expect, we are working with partners across government to make sure we can effectively support relevant sectors.”

data.title: One million risk losing landline as digital switchover looms
data.description:
Have you been overcharged, struggled to get a refund, dealt with poor customer service or spotted something consumers should know about? Get in touch with us in the comments or email consumeraffairs@telegraph.co.uk*.

One million customers have just three months to upgrade their analogue phone lines as part of a UK-wide digital switchover.

Landline operators are switching home phones across the country to internet-based connections instead of copper-wire cables.

BT-owned Openreach, which operates the UK’s largest landline network, is scheduled to shut down its old system on Jan 31.

It told The Telegraph that one million customers, comprising both residents and businesses, were still on the old public switched telephone network (PSTN) despite the looming cut-off date.

Some customers who miss the deadline may be moved on to a temporary emergency phone service which does not have features such as voicemail. Others risk losing their connection altogether.

James Lilley, Openreach director of customer migrations, said that tens of thousands of customers were switching each week, but a rise in scams had made it harder to get consumers to respond to letters about the change.

“It’s very hard to get [customers] to read and react and do something,” he said.

Recently published data from Openreach showed that London had the greatest proportion of legacy lines still left to switch among major UK cities.

Business owners would also be affected as the PSTN system supports some payment terminals, emergency phones in lifts and door entry systems.

Although the deadline is nearing, Openreach insisted there would not be a single day when customers suddenly lose access to services.

Mr Lilley said: “There is no big red button that will switch everyone off on Jan 31.”

But the back-up line, known as the emergency voice access (Evac) service, does not include certain other features, such as three-way calling or call diversion.

The industry had originally targeted a switch-off date of Dec 31, 2025. After concerns were raised about rural households and vulnerable, often elderly, customers who rely on telecare alarms, this was extended.

Under the PSTN Charter, providers agreed not to switch users of telecare devices unless their devices, such as fall alarms, were compatible with digital landlines.

Telecom companies, including BT, have also been giving free back-up battery packs to vulnerable customers who rely on their landlines, which can keep phones working for an hour or more.

Campaign group Silver Voices has, however, called for another extension, saying it was necessary to address the needs of older customers and businesses where there may be complex engineering problems.

Earlier this week, MPs also warned that the plans could leave people in remote areas unable to contact help in an emergency such as a severe storm or a cyber attack.

Unlike digital services, the traditional landline network does not rely on mains electricity and so continues to work in a power cut.

The Government has said the migration to digital, which was first announced in 2017, was necessary because the ageing copper-based network had become less reliable.

But during a debate in the Commons on Tuesday, Torcuil Crichton, a Labour MP, who represents the Western Isles constituency of Na h-Eileanan an Iar, said: “Resilience is inbuilt in the islands but we have major problems with connectivity because of this move from analogue to digital phone lines.

“When the power goes out, people don’t have the phone, they don’t have the internet and often they don’t have a mobile signal either,” he added.

Julian Lewis, a Conservative MP, also raised concerns about the lack of a “back-up system” if digital phone services were not available.

He told Dan Jarvis, the security minister, that the copper-wire network “could have given us useful levels of resilience in an emergency”.

Mr Jarvis said he would “look very closely” at this point.

Ofcom said it expected minimal disruption for most customers.

A spokesman for the regulator said that it has clear rules that phone companies must follow when switching customers to digital landlines.

It said it was monitoring the process closely and had already fined one firm for “putting vulnerable customers at unacceptable risk of harm” during the changeover.

A BT Group spokesman said: “As we focus on the small minority of our customers yet to make the switch, protecting those who need extra support remains our top priority.”

data.title: Trump rages at Fox News as Republican voters switch off
data.description:
As the results began to flood in on a bruising midterm election night for the Republicans, Donald Trump picked an unlikely scapegoat: Fox News.

The US president, evidently glued to Fox’s coverage, took aim at the channel’s polls and choice of guests in a slew of angry late-night posts on Truth Social.

“FoxNews bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse,” he wrote.

At the same time, he hit the network with a dig about its viewership. “FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats! All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It’s them, not me – My numbers are better than they have ever been.”

The comments came even as Trump called and texted into the Murdoch-owned news network, which has long been his biggest cheerleader and helped bring him to power. It underscores the complex, co-dependent relationship between the two.

The Democrats’ stunning midterms victory raises questions about Fox’s place in the media landscape, amid a sharp drop in ratings. Once an all-powerful force in US politics, its influence is fading.

A lame-duck Trump is ostensibly more bad news for the network. For all the talk of balance, no individual has come to embody Fox more than Trump. His bolshy and erratic behaviour has dominated the news agenda and provided news fodder for more than a third of the network’s life.

A spurred and vengeful Trump may present more fodder for the network, as will coverage of the wave of “far-Left” Democrats who have now come to power. But there is no guarantee that audiences will stick with them for these stories. Many have already jumped ship to YouTube or streamers.

For cable news networks, election nights are often compared to the Super Bowl as droves of viewers tune in for blow-by-blow updates. Fox even deployed a special chatbot providing real-time answers to audience questions.

The run-up to the midterms provided ample material, with Trump facing off against Barack Obama on the campaign trail in recent weeks.

Yet Fox’s ratings have been anything but blockbuster. Fox News attracted an average audience of 1.1 million in October, down 27pc compared to last year, according to official figures from Nielsen.

In primetime hours between 8pm and 11pm, Fox pulled in fewer than 1.7 million viewers, down from 2.3 million at the same time last year. The network looks set to record its worst-performing month for overall viewers since December 2023.

The decline has not escaped the attention of Fox bosses. Lachlan Murdoch, the 55-year-old scion whose ascension to the throne of the family empire was confirmed last year following a fraught succession battle, this week admitted that the network had been hit by “viewer fatigue”.

“It was a tremendous news cycle this time last year, which we’re comping against,” he told investors, pointing to events in 2025, including the assassination of Charlie Kirk.

Murdoch insisted that this was a broader trend, rather than a reflection on Fox specifically.

“Those viewers are not going to any other news channel,” he said. “They’re not switching to MS Now or to CNN. They’re just fatigued and watching slightly less television overall.”

Yet these claims are undermined by viewing figures for both CNN and MS Now – the network formerly known as MSNBC – which grew 19pc and 13pc in primetime respectively last month.

“Human nature is at play here, especially when it comes to political news consumption where people seek affirmation that ‘their side’ is right and winning when momentum is in their favour,” says Mike Proulx, an analyst at Forrester.

“When that’s not the case, people can shut down and seek an escape from reality, which results in news avoidance.”

Fox remains the largest cable news network. The company argues that its rivals are growing from a low comparison last year and say the network enjoyed its highest-rating midterm year ever despite the slump.

A spokesman said: “Fox News has been the number one network in cable news for a quarter century, throughout every administration since 2001.

“More recently, the network has expanded its dominance beyond linear, where it is not only the top-rated cable network on television, but dominates digital, streaming, social media and YouTube, generating nearly four billion YouTube video views this year alone.”

Nevertheless, the weakness during what should be a strong period for viewing figures points at a tougher future ahead.

Cable networks have for years been battling an exodus of audiences to streaming alternatives, known in the US as “cord-cutting”. Fox last year launched its own streaming service – Fox One – in an effort to counteract this trend.

Proulx says traditional TV has “lost its grip on non-boomer audiences”. A recent survey showed that while 44pc of US baby boomers said traditional TV takes up most of their weekly entertainment time, that figure tumbles to 19pc of Gen X, 5pc of millennials and only 3pc of Gen Z.

For Fox, these industry trends are exacerbated by its complex entanglement with Trump, an avid viewer of the channel.

Two prominent figures in the Trump administration – Pete Hegseth, the defence secretary, and Jeanine Pirro, the United States attorney for the District of Columbia – are former Fox hosts. Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s former White House press secretary, has joined Fox as a pundit and defended the president on election night.

In turn, the US president has been a rich source of material.

Trump’s 2016 election victory delivered a record audience, which was beaten only by the 14.1 million people who tuned in during the 2020 vote, when Murdoch’s network infuriated the president with an early call for Joe Biden in Arizona.

Other events, including Trump’s impeachment and attempted assassination, have also delivered major spikes in the channel’s audience, in a phenomenon described as the “Trump bump”.

“My view would be, based upon a decade of Trump as president with the Biden interregnum, that he is fantastic for news media,” says analyst Alex DeGroote. “He sets the news agenda every day, whether you like him or hate him.”

This has been handsomely profitable for Fox, which reported $350m (£260m) in political advertising revenue in its latest quarter, representing a record for the midterm period.

But Trump has blown hot and cold with his long-time ally Rupert Murdoch. A US judge last week dismissed Trump’s $10bn lawsuit against Murdoch’s Wall Street Journal over its reporting of a letter the president allegedly wrote to Jeffrey Epstein.

Fox was forced to cough up nearly $800m in 2023 to settle a defamation lawsuit over its reporting of Trump’s stolen election claims, showing the cost of unwavering support for the president.

With Trump now a lame duck, Fox’s ratings slump may worsen.

“I think the key question is: is this the beginning of a downward trend?” says DeGroote.

“He’s magnetic viewing, but we are closer to the end than the beginning, and it may well be that the second half of his presidency is less box-office than the first half.”

Conversely, if an angered Trump employs a scorched-earth policy it would create ever more headlines.

“I think you could make a case that we could be in for a real period of friction, which could lead to even more electric viewing and even more outlandish episodes,” says DeGroote.

The renewed power of the Democrats could also provide compulsive “hate-watching” for Fox’s core audience.

The network has repeatedly referred to Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat firebrand who has become the first Muslim US senator after his victory in Michigan, as “far-Left”.

More broadly, its coverage has painted a picture of a socialist takeover of the US Left, with stories highlighting divisions within the Democratic Party over progressive policies such as abolishing ICE and the proposed Medicare for All.

Tom Emmer, the Republican House majority whip, summed up the position during an appearance on Fox Business’s The Bottom Line, saying: “There’s nothing democratic about socialism.”

Yet Republicans may watch these dramas play out elsewhere. Some of the network’s most outspoken former stars, including Tucker Carlson and Megyn Kelly, have pursued their own shows on YouTube. Trump, who can reach his supporters directly via Truth Social, recently also launched his own channel on the streaming platform.

At the same time, Fox’s arch-rival on the other side of the political spectrum, CNN, is bracing for its own shake-up under the ownership of David Ellison, a Trump ally.

Industry watchers believe he could try to shift the editorial line of CNN. Ellison, who took control of the network following a $100bn merger between Paramount and Warner Bros, has already proven controversial for his editorial interference in CBS News.

Despite a calamitous night, Trump is not done yet. Nevertheless, with the end of his administration now in sight, bosses know the curtain will soon be coming down on the Trump show. It is a problem that Fox News executives must figures out how to confront.

“We’ll look back on this time in a few years and think it was the most extraordinary period ever,” says DeGroote.

“It will be very quiet and boring when Trump’s gone.”

data.title: Volvo loses £1bn in value as it slashes 2,500 jobs
data.description:
Volvo has announced plans to slash 2,500 jobs after a sharp fall in sales triggered a share price slump that has wiped £1bn from its value.

Shares in the company, which is owned by Chinese group Geely, plunged as much as 31pc after it revealed revenues fell by 23pc in the third quarter.

Volvo announced a 5bn Swedish kronor (£376.4m) cost-cutting plan that will result in around 2,000 job cuts in Sweden and another 500 globally “through natural attrition and by targeted exit packages to employees”.

The car manufacturer warned it may have to take “additional actions” after revenues in China fell by almost 50pc and it was hit by the loss of electric car subsidies in the US.

Volvo issued a profit warning and pulled its annual guidance earlier this month as sales declined.

Hakan Samuelsson, Volvo’s chief executive, said on Friday: “We continue to operate in a very tough environment with strong external challenges: de-globalisation, hypercompetition and climate change.

“The third quarter of 2026 was very disappointing and reflects a year that has become far more challenging than originally anticipated. Our ongoing turnaround plan therefore needs ​a decisive reinforcement.”

Volvo is the latest European car manufacturer to announce sweeping job losses. In July, BMW revealed it would cut 8,000 jobs in an attempt to reduce costs. Earlier this year, Volkswagen said it would cut as many as 100,000 roles out of a total workforce of 650,000. The move is expected to result in the closure of four factories.

Jaguar Land Rover, Britain’s largest car manufacturer, said in September that it would cut 4,000 jobs over the next two years.

Volvo’s revenues in the three months to the end of September slumped to 66.9bn Swedish kronor (£5bn), a 23pc decline from the same period a year earlier.

The car manufacturer also fell to a net loss of 5.7bn kronor (£429.2m) in the third quarter, down from a net profit of 4.5bn kronor (£338.8m) a year earlier.

Volvo, which had bet heavily on electric vehicle sales, said the axing of customer incentives in the US under Donald Trump had dented its revenue.

In 2024, the carmaker scrapped a target of transitioning to selling only electric cars by the end of the decade.

Last month, Volvo said that Mr Samuelsson would leave as chief executive next year, with Klaus Zellmer, the boss of Skoda Auto, due to take up the Volvo chief executive of the Swedish car manufacturer “no later” than October next year.

data.title: The 33-year-old at the forefront of Britain’s defence revolution
data.description:
To see the future of Britain’s defence industry, you have to visit a four-storey building found on what used to be a car park off Old Kent Road. This clean and functional edifice is the biggest new factory in London since the Second World War.

A Union Flag overlooks the factory floor, where 12 machines are silently engaged in turning steel, aluminium and titanium into precision components for jet engines, drones, robots and much more.

Presiding over them is Alexander Fitzgerald, the 33-year-old founder and chief executive of the company, Isembard, which he established in late 2024.

Like everyone who creates a successful business, the T-shirt-wearing entrepreneur spotted a problem and proposed a solution. “What’s happening across every single sector right now – from aerospace to defence to robotics to energy to semiconductors – is that demand is massively increasing, but the supply of manufacturing capacity to make those components is reducing,” he says.

Isembard’s driving purpose is to provide some of that desperately needed extra capacity. The opportunity is all the greater because of a revolution sweeping Britain’s defence industry.

For generations, the sector has been dominated by a handful of large “prime contractors”, such as BAE Systems, which specialise in the slow and hugely expensive production of a relative handful of advanced jet fighters, tanks and warships, designed to stay in service for decades.

But the lesson from Ukraine is that there are increasing – and critical – advantages for countries that can speedily produce an abundance of smaller and cheaper systems, such as drones, then constantly improve and redesign them, and turn out new and better models every few months. This requires a multitude of small and medium-sized enterprises that can compete to be the most innovative and efficient by deploying AI to make an ever-changing array of components as quickly and cheaply as possible.

Isembard is already doing exactly that. Companies send 3D designs for the parts they need, and Isembard manufactures them according to those designs. “We build our own software and AI to make setting up our factories and running our factories really efficient,” says Fitzgerald.

At present, about 95 per cent of components for manufacturing are produced by small and medium-scale businesses. It is an extraordinary fact that the average age of the owners of these companies in the UK is 65 – and that no less than 40 per cent of them plan to retire within five years.

At the exact moment when Europe is rearming – with all Nato countries, including Britain, pledging to spend at least 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence by 2035 – the supply chain for new components is contracting.

Hence, Isembard is expanding rapidly to meet pent-up demand. Fitzgerald opened his first factory last year, and today his company has 18 worldwide – eight in Britain, eight in America and one each in France and Germany.

This growth has been accelerated by Isembard’s unique business model, which allows for franchised factories. All but five of the existing plants are not owned by the company, but franchised to individual operators. The newest, in Swindon, took a mere 90 days to set up, and Fitzgerald aims to get this down to one or two weeks.

Speed and agility are everything. Fitzgerald notes that what has allowed Ukraine to resist the Russian invaders is not one kind of exquisitely engineered drone, but rather a vast and constantly changing array of different models. “In Ukraine, it’s not one type of drone – and 10 billion of them,” he says. “It’s a zoo of different types of drones, at all classes and all stages. Then you need to be able to scale up.”

Fitzgerald adds: “You need a manufacturing base, which is fundamentally a question of, ‘Have you got enough stuff that can make stuff? Have you networked them enough to be more efficient?’ That’s really the core of our business.”

Reindustrialising Britain by reshoring production is, he believes, the key to the country’s future prosperity. “The grand theory of everything is manufacturing because it’s the root of our prosperity, security and purpose,” he says. “I subscribe to the manufacturing dream – that means security and prosperity [depend on] your ability to make stuff.”

Nearby, the computer numerical control (CNC) machines – which have affectionate nicknames such as Cathy and Big Bertha – on the factory floor are playing their part in reindustrialising Britain by turning out the precisely shaped objects that will soon be flying at high speed as the components of jet engines or drones.

The factory, which covers three floors and 160,000 square feet, aims to triple its workforce to 200 by the end of next year. Taking delivery of the hulking CNCs required Fitzgerald to install a bigger loading door in the building, which was previously used as a grocery depot. The machines had to arrive in the early hours of the morning, since there are timing restrictions within three miles of Charing Cross for loads of that weight and size.

Fitzgerald emphasises that Isembard is not a “defence tech company”, but rather a “manufacturing company”. About 60 per cent of its customers are in aerospace and defence, while most of the rest are in robotics.

But Russia is unlikely to be interested in that distinction as its intelligence services carry out their escalating campaign of sabotage and subversion across Europe, including in Britain.

Is Fitzgerald concerned about that threat? “Yes, and I think the Government should be concerned,” he replies. “We have good security protections in both the cyber and the physical side. We’ve had a lot of support from the Government, and from the police and other agencies, as well.”

Fitzgerald has personal experience of Whitehall, since he spent three years as a Treasury civil servant after graduating from Nottingham University with a degree in biochemistry. Earlier, he had also tried his hand at journalism as an intern at City AM.

He enjoyed his time working in the Government, but cannot help remembering: “When I thought I had the right answer for something, it still had to go through six pairs of hands to get to someone to make a decision. That frustrated me.”

He left the Treasury to start a broadband company that amassed almost 100,000 customers before he sold it to Octopus Group in 2022. Fitzgerald founded Isembard soon afterwards, and the company now makes components for customers like Anduril, which manufactures drones and autonomous weaponry, and Oxford Space Systems, which produces the antennae for satellites.

In the past, certain British investors and banks had a fastidious disdain for any businesses linked to defence, some of which were denied financial services. Fitzgerald, who is also an Army reservist, has encountered no such difficulties, and he believes that attitudes have changed. “I think Ukraine has changed that,” he says. “Geopolitics has changed that.”

Something else that has changed is the attitude towards manufacturing in general. One of Andy Burnham’s central priorities is “reindustrialisation” and recapturing the dynamism of former years.

In that spirit, Fitzgerald named his company after the great Victorian engineer, Isambard Kingdom Brunel, though he adapted the spelling of his hero’s Christian name because the original domain had already been taken.

Today, he keeps a black top hat on his desk in tribute to the man whose individual drive and genius powered Britain’s first industrial revolution.

His other inspiration is Lord Beaverbrook, the minister for aircraft production in 1940, who galvanised British industry into delivering 100 Spitfires and Hurricanes every week, making him an architect of victory in the Battle of Britain and changing the course of the Second World War.

“The Air Ministry didn’t like him. He was threatening to resign the whole time, but he got the job done,” says Fitzgerald, who notes that Beaverbrook tripled production in a matter of months by distributing the manufacture of Spitfire and Hurricane components between hundreds of superbly innovative and cost-efficient small and medium enterprises across the country.

That formula saved Britain in 1940. It might yet do the same again.

data.title: Radio stations demand compensation for terrestrial TV switch-off
data.description:
British radio stations are demanding compensation to cover soaring costs if ministers switch off terrestrial TV in the next decade.

The commercial operators behind stations such as Heart, Magic and Classic FM are pushing for a “mitigation package” amid concerns the transition to streaming could force them off air.

The Government has said there is a “compelling” case for switching off terrestrial signals in 2034, though some campaigners are calling for this to be delayed until 2044.

While the discussions have been focused primarily on TV broadcasters such as the BBC, ITV and Channel 4, radio bosses have warned that the transition poses a critical threat to their future.

This is because radio stations would be left to cover the costs of the energy-intensive masts that they share with TV channels.

Recent research commissioned by industry body Radiocentre found that transmission costs for radio broadcasters could increase by more than 50pc if the switch-off goes ahead in 2034.

Industry figures estimate that covering the additional costs would run into the tens of millions of pounds per year.

They have argued that the switch-off should be delayed unless a suitable compensation package can be implemented.

Matt Payton, the chief executive of Radiocentre, said: “Commercial radio stations face huge cost increases if the switch-off goes ahead in 2034. This could end up putting services at risk and will be deeply unpopular with audiences, who also stand to lose access to their favourite TV channels.

“Radio plays a crucial role in delivering trusted information, particularly during emergencies. If the Government wants to secure this for the future, it needs to put in place a suitable cost mitigation package for radio or delay this change entirely.”

In its green paper published over the summer, the Government acknowledged that any transition would need to include a plan to mitigate the effects on the radio industry.

The fallout from the terrestrial switch-off is also being examined in a separate review into the future of British radio, which is expected to publish its findings by the end of the year.

It is not clear whether the Government would fund any compensation or whether broadcasters would be asked to contribute.

Any such move would probably trigger a row with Britain’s beleaguered broadcasters, which are pushing for an early switch-off as viewers move online.

Campaigners argue that an early switch to streaming only risks leaving elderly and vulnerable audiences behind.

However, the campaign promoting this view is being heavily backed by Arqiva, the debt-laden monopoly that owns Britain’s TV masts and has a significant commercial interest in extending their lifespan.

Its latest accounts, published this week, showed Arqiva crashed to a £1.8bn loss in the year to the end of June, driven by a major impairment on the value of its broadcasting infrastructure and interest payments on its debt pile of £9.8bn.

A Government spokesman said it understood that switching off terrestrial broadcast would affect radio and was looking at the future of the sector more broadly.

They added: “The Government believes there is a strong case for a long-term transition to Internet Protocol Television but no decisions have been made. We are gathering views from across the sector and the public before any final decisions are taken.”

data.title: Burnham has backed himself into a corner over public control of Thames Water
data.description:
The quest to save Thames Water is the saga with no end. Two and a half years after shareholders abandoned the company, its future is no more certain.

On the contrary, it is even more of a financial basket-case now than it was then, having been kept afloat by a steady drip-feed of emergency loans at a business that was already drowning in debt.

Additional borrowings since March 2024 stand at roughly £3bn with another £2.4bn on the cards, just to see it through the next 12 months.

That assumes, of course, that a disparate creditor base can agree on a deal – far from a foregone conclusion despite the high stakes.

The arrival of Andy Burnham in No 10 would bring an end to this financial purgatory, we were told.

Under Showtime Andy a privately led, debt-heavy industry ownership model that prioritised shareholder enrichment rather than customer care would be consigned to the dustbin, replaced by a system of greater “public control” – even though no one in Government has been able to explain what that means.

Burnham’s intervention has been characteristically cack-handed. Instead of steadying the ship, the Prime Minister has done precisely the opposite, exacerbating the uncertainty.

The problem is his propensity to speak first without thinking about the consequences. Just three months into his Premiership, a clear pattern has already been established: Burnham’s desire to be popular means he cannot help but put his foot in his mouth.

On Thames Water, he has backed himself into the tightest of corners. Burnham’s enthusiasm for nationalisation was such that it was widely assumed it would be among the first truly meaningful things the former mayor of Manchester would do upon setting foot in Downing Street.

The problem is that nobody in government, including the Prime Minister, paused to consider whether such a move was even plausible. Everyone was too concerned with playing to the gallery, telling an exasperated British public what it was assumed it wanted to hear.

But as ministers have quickly discovered, there is a big difference between wanting to do something and being able to, and the reality is that he inherited a country that cannot afford public ownership of critical assets such as Thames.

Some Labour figures have allowed themselves to be fooled into thinking that the Government could simply seize control without having to buy out the creditors.

But as has been pointed out, including in this column, such a move would amount to expropriation, something more associated with failing Communist regimes.

It’s fine to talk about wanting to end neoliberalism, but the reality is that the UK economy is massively reliant on foreign capital, much of it from long-term investors of the sort that had been lending to Thames long before the Wall Street hedge funds turned up.

Government contempt for the rule of law and property rights would be devastating to this country’s standing.

But even if Thames could be nationalised without recourse to the creditors, there is another glaring flaw that the pro-nationalisation crowd are unable to address: where will the investment come from afterwards?

There can be no doubt that water suppliers and their many shareholders are guilty of woeful underinvestment in the industry stretching back many years, something that a supine regulator must take some of the responsibility for.

But the country’s decrepit Victorian pipes and filthy waterways require a staggering £290bn of funding in the next 25 years just to ensure the taps stay on and our rivers are cleaned up.

These are figures from the National Audit Office, which also points out that at the current rate, it would take 700 years to renew the entire network.

Does this Government have that sort of money lying around? Of course not – not even close. It’s preposterous to even suggest that nationalisation of the water sector, or even just Thames, is somehow feasible.

Yet having seen his rhetoric collide with reality, the Prime Minister refuses to accept defeat. Officials are being told to come up with other ideas that would enable him to claim his promise of greater public control has been achieved.

The latest half-cocked plan supposedly on the table is to convert £100m of fines into a government stake, but a fag-packet calculation suggests that would equate to around 3pc of the company.

Not only is that close to meaningless, the creditors would still own the vast majority of it – something Labour MPs have made it clear they are vehemently opposed to.

It would also mean letting the company off a slew of fines for pollution when ministers have made a big song and dance about ensuring irresponsible water suppliers are properly held to account for any damage to the environment.

The result is a dangerous stalemate that will come back to bite the Prime Minister.

Burnham refuses to give his blessing to a restructuring proposal that’s been on the table for 18 months and will result in billions of pounds of Thames Water’s debts written off along with billions more in fresh equity pumped into the business.

Yet he and his team are yet to come up with any credible alternatives.

If the hedge funds aren’t the answer, and the Government doesn’t have a plan B, then what instead?

Wouldn’t a better solution be one in which the private sector continues to provide the vast financial resources required but under a regime of greater outside oversight and governance?

This can be done without the need for full nationalisation or for the state to have any economic interest at all.

Thames Water’s creditors have already agreed to a dividend freeze. They are willing to give the Government a golden share too, and the idea of allowing local mayors to have representation on its board has been floated too.

There could be an employee representative as well, which is the model in many European countries. Perhaps the privately held suppliers could also be partially floated on the stock exchange, a move that would guarantee much greater transparency and scrutiny.

There are many versions of this, but the Government urgently needs to clarify what its position is.

The longer Thames is left in limbo, the greater the risk that the vilified investors who have been propping it up will lose patience and walk away, leaving the Government to attempt to contain the fallout. This includes ensuring services aren’t interrupted.

If that happens, ministers will be responsible for one of the most spectacular slow-motion car crashes of all time.

data.title: Veterans forced to take 5am rail replacement bus to Remembrance Sunday
data.description:
Veterans have been offered a rail replacement bus at nearly 5am to reach Remembrance Sunday events in London.

Major Christopher McLean, 67, from Wiltshire, said the arrangements were “not good enough” and would prevent fellow veterans attending memorials.

In an email seen by The Telegraph, the Royal British Legion warned Cenotaph Parade ticket-holders that rail engineering works would bring disruption on Nov 8.

The charity advised veterans that South Western Railway and Network Rail Wessex were offering limited one-way bus travel from Winchester and Salisbury railway stations that were departing at 4.45am to arrive at London Waterloo at 8am.

Scheduled replacement bus services are also operating, requiring changes between rail and bus services to arrive in London on time.

Major McLean, who lives outside Salisbury, told The Telegraph that the disruption meant he would have to get up at 3.45am, which was not ideal at his age.

“No one seems to have thought this through,” he told The Telegraph, adding: “If I had planned like that in my Army logistics career, I would have been sacked.”

Veterans forced to ‘make other arrangements’

Major McLean said that veterans would be prevented attending events in the capital because of the disruption.

He said: “Lots of us are in our 70s. What about the implications for people who are infirm? It’s not good enough. Most of the guys I know are going to have to make other arrangements.

“Luckily, I can go up the night before and stay with relatives in Surrey. If I hadn’t had family there, I would have pulled out.

“Others are looking at paying for two nights in a London hotel, which is expensive. The Royal British Legion does a great job getting this all together, but the wider logistics haven’t been considered properly.”

Veterans would have been able to leave closer to 7am if the trains were running. This would still have allowed them enough time to arrive in Whitehall, pass through police security procedures and form up on the Cenotaph for 10.30am.

Major McLean said the rail disruption was the latest woe to be bestowed on veterans.

He said: “Prosecutions of veterans, underfunding of defence – it’s one thing after another, which is really upsetting this community. This is the latest mark of disrespect.”

Veteran’s fiercely oppose Labour’s Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, which is currently in the House of Lords, arguing that it does not adequately protect former service members.

Col Richard Kemp, a retired British Army officer who served from 1977 to 2006, criticised the lack of foresight by the railway operators.

“This is probably the most important day of the year when people can come together and pay respects to the war dead,” he said, adding: “It should be given priority above other events.

“Veterans should be treated with the utmost respect, including by the railway companies. This clearly isn’t good enough.”

Last month, the Government announced that it was extending free railway travel on Remembrance weekend, which currently covers serving military staff, veterans and one next of kin of a service-person who died while serving.

However, networks across the country will be disrupted by engineering work on Nov 7 and 8.

South Western Railway, the first operator to be renationalised by Labour in May 2025, apologised to veterans whose journeys would be affected.

A spokesman said: “South Western Railway is proud of its commitment to the Armed Forces community and this year received the Ministry of Defence Gold Award.

“Unfortunately, long-planned and essential engineering works this weekend mean veterans will need to use a combination of train and rail replacement services to travel to London Waterloo.

“We investigated whether the engineering works could be rescheduled, but this would have meant deferring essential track maintenance to maintain the long-term safety and reliability of the railway.”

A spokesman for the Royal British Legion said: “We’ve worked with the rail authorities to contact veterans affected by planned engineering works so they know a rail replacement service has been arranged.”

data.title: Twelve flights diverted across Europe after bomb threats
data.description:
Twelve flights have been diverted across Europe following a series of bomb threats.

Thursday’s disruption comes days after similar incidents in which eight planes, including three from the UK, were grounded over what Britain dismissed as a “malicious hoax”.

Three of Thursday’s incidents involved flights bound for Italy.

An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to Normandy following a bomb alert, the French prime minister’s office said.

The office of Sébastien Lecornu, the French prime minister, said all 151 passengers and six crew members were safe, and that military bomb defusal teams were examining the plane.

A Finnair flight bound for Helsinki landed in Rome after a threat was reported on board, while a Wizz Air service from Milan Malpensa to Warsaw was diverted to Vienna.

A Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed at Zaventem airport in Belgium after the crew received a “suspicious report concerning a flight to Brussels airport”.

Three more aircraft were forced to land at airports in Bulgaria following bomb threats. 

Two of the planes – travelling from Copenhagen and Madrid respectively – landed in Sofia, the broadcaster bTV, citing the interior minister, reported.

A third aircraft, flying from London, landed in Plovdiv, according to reports. Four planes flying to Prague had been the subject of bomb threats and were preparing to land, according to Czech police. 

A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest was also targeted, Romanian intelligence services said.

On Thursday morning, Spanish authorities said three flights at Madrid were affected by hoax threats.

None of the threats reported this week have been found to be genuine, despite triggering dozens of unplanned landings as well and escorts by fighter jets.

The EU’s transport commissioner said it was “too early to draw conclusions” on whether Thursday’s spate of bomb threats were linked.

Apostolos Tzitzikostas said in a message posted on LinkedIn that he had asked EU security authorities “to cooperate closely with airport operators, airlines and law enforcement authorities” over the bomb threats.

On Tuesday, at least seven planes were subjected to threats. A flight to Sofia was similarly affected on Monday.

An airport in Warsaw was briefly shut and the Italian air force accompanied one of the flights to Rome. An Israel-bound cruise ship was also searched for bombs in Greece.

A British Government spokesman told The Telegraph that the threats against the UK flights had been a “malicious hoax”, though it was not clear how they had been orchestrated.

Speculation quickly centred on Moscow, with a former MI6 intelligence officer telling The Telegraph that it was his first thought when he learned of the bomb threats, which he said fitted “a pattern of behaviour” by the Kremlin.

The flight disruption follows a week of chaos, with dozens of supermarket fridges across Europe hacked on Monday. The attacks caused large amounts of food to spoil after hackers gained remote access to in-store fridge units and turned up their temperatures, in some cases to as much as 80C.

Hackers also targeted France’s national blood bank, raising the temperature of its cold storage rooms to boiling point.

Facilities at Coolworld were heated to 110C overnight on Sunday after hackers gained access to the temperature settings remotely, Le Canard enchaîné reported. The rooms are normally kept at -30C to preserve donor blood samples.

An on-duty technician detected the unusual rise in temperatures. France’s health ministry said there had been no consequences for patients and no plasma had been destroyed.

The Kremlin said European media accusations of Russian involvement in ‌cyber attacks on supermarkets were not backed up by any evidence.

Dmitry ⁠Peskov, a Kremlin spokesman, told reporters on Thursday: “These are absurd claims. As always, they are backed up by absolutely ‌no reasoning, no evidence whatsoever, and yet here we have ⁠such ⁠baseless accusations against our country, implicating it in everything.”

However, pro-Russian hackers have claimed responsibility for the cyber attacks on fridges.

The pro-Russian hacking collective NoName057(16) claimed to have worked with Z-Pentest, another pro-Russian hacker group, to launch the attack.

A video claiming responsibility for the attack was posted on Telegram, according to the Danish media outlet DR.

In the video, titled Operation Chronicle: Danfoss, the hackers claimed to have “dealt a crushing blow to Danfoss and Dixell XWEB equipment”.

Danfoss and Dixell XWEB were the refrigeration companies targeted in the cyber attack.

“We didn’t even need malware for that. We just exploited the systems’ built-in features,” the hackers said.

data.title: M&S lashes out at Labour over ‘one of the biggest tax grabs in history’
data.description:
The boss of Marks & Spencer has accused Labour of unleashing “one of the biggest tax grabs in history” in an outspoken attack on the Government.

Stuart Machin, the chief executive of M&S, said the retailer was having to navigate an “onslaught” of higher costs and stricter regulations as a direct result of the three Budgets delivered by Rachel Reeves and John Healey.

Mr Machin said the retailer faced an extra £150m in costs this year, mostly from Labour’s 2024 Budget.

This includes an extra £50m in employers’ National Insurance Contributions, £50m from above-inflation increases in the National Minimum Wage, and up to £40m of new packaging taxes.

M&S also faces additional costs related to the conflict in the Middle East.

Mr Machin said: “In terms of the Budget overall, I think we all know, it was a whole lot of nothing.

“When you look at the last three Budgets, you just can’t ignore the fact that this is probably one of the biggest tax grabs in history that I’ve seen. And of course, that does mean from our perspective that more tax and more regulatory burden just adds so much extra cost and complexity to business.” 

John Healey’s maiden Budget raised taxes by £6.97bn, while his predecessor Rachel Reeves oversaw £67.82bn of tax rises across her two Budgets, altogether totalling £74.79bn.

Mr Machin said the £40m impact of new packaging regulations and taxes that came into force in April wiped out all food profits that month.

He added that he was “disappointed” with Mr Healey’s Budget last week because “it didn’t really address the issues that we needed to focus on growth”.

Even the Chancellor’s freeze on business rates would add another £10m to the retailer’s existing business rates bill of £170m, he said.

Mr Machin warned: “When you think of [policies] coming down the road, I can’t see things getting any better.”

He singled out the “ridiculous” deposit return scheme for plastic and aluminium drinks containers coming into force next October.

One of Britain’s most respected bosses, Mr Machin has been a frank critic of Labour’s business policies, once describing the previous two Budgets as “a disaster”.

‘Can’t ignore’ hacking threat

He spoke as M&S released first-half results showing a strong recovery from last year’s cyber attack. The high street giant revealed pre-tax profits of £403.2m for the six months to Sept 26, in line with City analysts’ forecasts.

This was more than double the £184.1m recorded last year, when a disastrous cyber attack ravaged the company’s performance and forced it to stop all online sales for six weeks.

However, it was still well below the £671.4m reported in the previous year.

Mr Machin said there had been no further incidents but added it would be “naive” to assume hackers would not try again, particularly in light of the recent cyber attacks on supermarket fridges across Europe.

He said: “We can’t ignore it, and we’ve got to manage the risk and also be prepared for any of those things happening and how we recover.”

He added that the turnaround of the non-food division remained “in the foothills” amid challenging market conditions, particularly for fashion, where results fell short of expectations.

Non-food operating profits of £150.5m were a strong recovery from last year’s £46.1m but still trailed the £243.4m seen in 2024.

The company blamed “availability disruption reflecting the long-tail impact of the incident and lower store sales during the prolonged summer heat”.

However, food sales grew by 13.9pc, delivering an operating profit of £288.6m, compared with £89.1m last year and well above the £216.4m achieved in 2024.

Grocery sales through M&S’s joint venture with online supermarket Ocado were up 22.8pc.

Mr Machin said the company had invested £50m in 300 “key family staples” in the first half of the year, with price reductions including a 500g pack of diced beef down to £6 and a pack of free-range eggs at £1.40.
