data.title: Virgin Media O2 ‘to axe 4,000 jobs’
data.description:
Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) is gearing up to cut thousands of jobs as it looks to tackle its burgeoning £22bn debt pile.

The telecoms giant is reportedly drawing up plans to cut 25pc of its 16,000-strong workforce.

Final details are expected in the company’s third quarter results due on Tuesday, with 4,000 job losses expected, Sky News reported.

Most affected jobs are understood to be non-customer facing, with changes in senior management also planned.

Unions including the Communication Workers Union (CWU) and Prospect have been briefed. Job cuts on such a scale would normally involve full consultations with unions and staff.

VMO2 was formed in June 2021 through a £31bn joint-venture merger between Spain’s Telefónica and Liberty Global, a Bermuda-domiciled multi-national with head offices in London, to challenge rival BT.

The Financial Times reported in September that VMO2’s parent companies were considering cuts in operating expenditure after a sell-off of its bonds during the summer left investors worried about its ability to service its debt pile.

Cuts to its £200m dividend were also on the table, the newspaper said.

The reported plans come just days after Lutz Schüler, the VMO2 chief executive, criticised Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, for backing BT’s £400m takeover of rival TalkTalk, which had been at risk of imminent collapse.

In a letter seen by The Telegraph, Mr Schüler wrote: “Protecting customers does not, in our view, require government to predetermine who should ultimately own TalkTalk’s consumer and wholesale businesses; credible alternative arrangements should be fully explored.

“Given the exceptional intervention, we would welcome clarity on the evidence relied upon by the secretary of state.”

VMO2 has been loaded with debt since its creation when Liberty Global (then the owner of Virgin Media) and Telefónica (then the owner of O2) agreed to merge their UK operations into a 50:50 joint venture.

Virgin Media was carrying roughly £11bn in net debt while O2 UK had virtually none. It meant that to make the combined company exactly 50:50, the joint venture had to borrow billions – meaning it was saddled with about £18bn in debt from day one.

The rise in interest rates subsequent to that deal meant the company has struggled with debt ever since.

In a provisional decision earlier this month, the Competition and Markets Authority said that an attempt by the parent companies of VMO2 to acquire Netomnia for £2bn could push up prices. A final decision on the deal is due in December.

Mike Fries, the chief executive of Liberty Global, warned in March that the company could stop building broadband in the UK if the deal was blocked.

In the 18 months to the end of June, VMO2 shed more than 170,000 customers, leaving 5.42 million remaining.

VMO2 is not the only telecoms giant making job cuts, with BT Group and VodafoneThree also in the midst of significant layoffs.

BT unveiled plans in 2023 to shed as much as a quarter of its then 130,000-strong workforce by 2030, partly driven by AI.

VodafoneThree announced 1,200 job losses across Europe earlier this year as part of a cost-cutting drive to save £700m annually by 2030.

Virgin Media O2 declined to comment. The CWU was contacted for comment.

Noel McClean, the deputy general secretary of Prospect, said: “Reports of expected job losses at VMO2 will be both disappointing and very unsettling for the staff who work there.

“When faced with redundancies, Prospect is committed to supporting our members through what is a difficult time, as well as also working with employers to explore ways to mitigate the number of redundancies and ensure retraining and redeployment of staff affected.”

data.title: Britain’s saving habit has collapsed. That hurts all of us
data.description:
Something bad is happening to Britain’s ability to save money. It’s a change that could have profound consequences for our economy, our politics and the sort of country we are. Yet it has attracted remarkably little attention.

Buried in last week’s Budget forecasts was a striking prediction from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR). By 2031, British households will be saving essentially nothing.

More precisely, the OBR expects that – excluding pension contributions – the proportion of disposable income that households save will fall from around 5.5 per cent last year to just 0.5 per cent in five years’ time.

Put another way, for every £100 of post-tax income they get, British households will be spending more than £99.50.

That would be the lowest level of saving in 25 years but the reason for this expected fall is more important than the numbers themselves. Normal economic analysis says that households save less – and borrow more – as their optimism about the future grows. When we think we’ll get richer in future, we have the confidence to spend more and save less.

But this isn’t what the nation’s official forecaster is predicting. Instead, the OBR believes that savings will all but disappear for miserable reasons. As we endure more years of stagnant real wages, the only way to maintain our spending is to save less.

The fact that pension saving is excluded from the OBR’s adjusted measure is important – largely thanks to auto-enrolled workplace pensions, people will go on saving at least something towards later life even when times are tough. But that money is prudently put out of reach until 55 or later. The downside of prudence is that these are savings that can’t help when the car breaks down or the washing machine packs up.

While economic pessimism is sadly common across Europe, this is a very British problem. James Smith, an economist at the Dutch bank ING, has calculated that once pension-related financial flows are excluded, British households are already more likely to be net borrowers rather than savers.

On ING’s estimates, British households last year saved 5 per cent of disposable income excluding pensions. In Germany, the figure was 17 per cent. Even allowing for economic and cultural differences – Germans rent rather than buy, and celebrate thrift above all else – our savings behaviour is precarious.

Precarious, but not unprecedented. Household saving declined sharply during the consumer boom of the late 1980s, when financial deregulation made borrowing easier and rising house prices made people feel richer. Something similar happened in the years before the 2007 financial crisis.

But this time is different. Those episodes were associated with economic confidence and expanding credit. Today’s decline in savings is born of gloom.

The decline should worry us for several reasons.

First, it means households will become less resilient. Savings help us withstand financial shocks: redundancy, illness, divorce, unexpected bills. Without savings, routine bad luck becomes disastrous, sometimes starting a spiral of expensive emergency borrowing from which a family’s finances never recover.

It is commonly estimated – especially by Labour MPs, who all know this figure by heart – that more than 11 million Britons have savings of less than £1,000. A collapse in the savings rate means that situation is unlikely to improve in the near future.

At a macroeconomic level, this lack of resilience means consumer spending – a vital motor of growth – is extremely fragile. Another cost-of-living shock could have disastrous consequences for a savings-light Britain.

The end of saving is also a serious problem for politicians.

Governments have become increasingly accustomed to taxing the income generated by household savings. Higher interest rates and frozen tax thresholds have dragged millions more savers into paying tax on interest. The latest Budget increases savings-income tax rates further, a reminder that savings are often a cash cow for the Treasury. Those OBR forecasts show the cow is now on a crash diet.

That’s also bad news for parts of Britain’s financial services industry, arguably our most important sector. Banks and investment managers rarely enjoy public affection but they play a vital role by ensuring that household savings support the lending and investment that helps power long-term growth. Less money flowing into their savings products is bad news for the wider economy.

The worst aspect of a country that doesn’t save is social and almost philosophical. Working hard should be a path to wealth, a path paved with savings. The wages put aside after spending should allow a worker to acquire assets that grow in value and deliver a return. That’s often a house, but ideally it would also be shares and other financial assets too: the old ideal of the property-owning democracy should start with a broad definition of property. A share-owning democracy would give us a better economy where more people have a stake in success.

The US has long known this. Now even Europeans are following. ING calculates that across the eurozone, consumers now allocate as much of their savings to investment funds as to cash deposits and pensions, something the bank sees as evidence of “a growing appetite for DIY investing”. Yet Britain is missing out on that shift.

If a worker has no spare money left to save at the end of the month, the idea of taking a stake in the economy becomes a fantasy. Without saving, assets remain out of reach and it is impossible to work your way to wealth. Without saving, only those born with wealth – or who inherit it – end up with assets, and the economic advantages they deliver.

What can be done to save savings? There are two things governments can do to help ensure people have some money left at the end of the month.

The simplest is to take less of that money in tax, ideally at the same time as offering more incentives to invest some of your savings in things like shares. The bigger, harder task is to address the reason people don’t have enough money left. Their wages aren’t growing fast enough to get ahead of prices.

Fixing Britain’s stagnant household incomes should have been a priority for years now, but the collapse in saving that stagnation should add new urgency. Giving up on saving will allow households to support consumption and living standards for only so long. A grim situation can still get worse.

data.title: Summer heatwaves caused blackouts, admits National Grid
data.description:
Soaring temperatures triggered a rise in energy blackouts during the summer, the National Grid admitted.

The utility giant told investors on Thursday that its network suffered “additional localised outages” in June, July and August, as the heat disrupted the infrastructure distributing power to homes and businesses.

National Grid revealed details of the blackouts in its latest half-year results on Thursday.

“In UK Electricity Distribution, network stability was maintained, but additional localised outages were experienced because of the significant increase in extreme heat during the UK summer period,” the company said.

The admission comes after one of the grid’s toughest summers.

Power networks typically come under heightened pressure during cold, still winter evenings, but multiple heatwaves created a supply pinch this year.

In early August, National Grid Electricity Distribution issued formal alerts and text messages directly to customers across the Midlands and the South, warning that power cuts were increasingly probable.

National Grid’s distribution business is responsible for powering 19 million homes across the East and West Midlands, South Wales and South West England, operating 137,000 miles of lines and cables.

Much of its infrastructure is decades old, leaving it more vulnerable to extreme weather.

Sustained heat prevents underground cables and transformers from cooling overnight, significantly increasing the risk of trips and faults.

Further disruption

The UK’s 14 distribution networks carry power from the high-voltage transmission system to homes and businesses. In England and Wales, the transmission system is owned by National Grid but managed day to day by the National Energy System Operator (Neso).

In June and July, Neso was forced to issue a series of “margin warnings” seeking extra supplies to meet rising demand for air conditioning and other cooling products.

Neso said that no blackouts occurred in July and August, but reports since have highlighted how precarious the situation was.

Whistleblowers from within Neso’s control room alleged that the grid operator underplayed how fragile margins were during the June heatwave, prompting an independent inquiry that raised issues over transparency.

National Grid’s latest admission will heighten concern that the UK is becoming increasingly vulnerable to weather-related disruption.

This is partially because of climate change, but experts also point to a growing reliance on intermittent renewables and the Grid’s ageing infrastructure.

This came to the fore last year when a major fire broke out at National Grid Electricity Transmission’s North Hyde substation in Hayes, west London.

The blaze erupted when an insulating component failed on one of the main transformers, igniting approximately 25,000 litres of cooling oil.

Nearby residents were evacuated as emergency crews tackled the fire, which cut power to 67,000 domestic and commercial customers.

Crucially, the outage severed the primary supply to Heathrow and three major data centres, forcing the airport to shut down for a day.

A subsequent investigation led by Neso, Ofgem and the London Fire Brigade found that the fire was caused by water entering the transformer – a problem detected seven years previously but left unresolved by National Grid.

National Grid said it had “taken further action” to strengthen its operations since the fire, such as carrying out additional risk assessments and retesting the resilience of substations.

data.title: BT loses £200m as households ditch landlines
data.description:
BT is facing a £200m hit as customers give up their landlines during a digital switchover.

The telecoms giant said it expected revenues to be between £150m and £200m lower this year as some customers ditch their landlines rather than switch to a digital alternative.

BT said the decline was temporary and would be offset by higher take-up of its full-fibre services, while the cost of supporting customers would also fall as the switchover completes.

It came as BT shed a further 18,000 jobs over the last six months, driven by a reduction in the number of engineers needed as it reaches the end of its full-fibre broadband rollout. Total headcount stood at 90,000 at the end of September.

Landline operators are moving customers from the old copper-wire network, known as the public switched telephone network, to modern connections delivered over the internet.

BT moved 1.1 million customers over the first half of the year. However, it warned that around one million homes or businesses still rely on old copper cables, with three months to go until the switch-off at the end of January.

A BT spokesman said: “More than three million households have now made the move to a digital landline, benefitting from a safer, more reliable service ahead of the industry‑wide analogue switchover in January 2027.

“As we focus on the small minority of our customers yet to make the switch, protecting those who need extra support remains our top priority.”

The looming deadline has prompted fears that some households and businesses could be left behind.

Some customers who fail to switch by the end of January will be placed on a temporary emergency phone service, but others risk being cut off altogether.

The transition was originally scheduled to be completed by the end of 2025, but the deadline was pushed back amid fears that elderly customers were being put at risk.

Two Virgin Media O2 customers died after their telecare devices stopped working following the switchover, while concerns have also been raised that digital landlines are more vulnerable to outages in the event of storms or cyber-attacks.

Providers have begun giving customers battery packs that can keep their landlines running during a power failure.

BT is also in discussions with the Government and Ofcom about a wider switch-off of its copper network that would also include broadband connections.

As a result of the additional costs, BT’s service revenue is expected to stand between £15.1bn and £15.4bn for the full year, compared with £15.4bn last year.

However, BT reported its first revenue increase in two and a half years, and pre-tax profit also rose in the six-month period, suggesting its turnaround plans are starting to pay off.

Higher handset sales drove the performance, while BT cut £312m in costs in the first half of the year, putting it halfway to its £3.5bn target.

BT’s Openreach division shed a further 366,000 broadband customers in the first half of the year amid fierce competition from start-up rivals, though this marked an improvement on last year’s losses.

BT also passed 10 million connections on its full-fibre network and is on track to hit its target of reaching 25 million homes in March.

Shares rose 5pc after bosses increased the interim dividend to 2.5p per share.

It comes at a turbulent time for Britain’s fiercely competitive broadband market as rivals including Virgin Media O2 and CityFibre grapple with the soaring costs of their debt-fuelled network rollouts.

BT last month struck a £400m deal to rescue stricken broadband provider TalkTalk, with ministers stepping in to override competition concerns.

The deal is undergoing a regulatory review, and Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, is expected to issue a final decision shortly.

data.title: Water bosses lose bonuses after worst pollution on record
data.description:
Several water bosses will be blocked from receiving bonuses after their companies were awarded the worst possible environmental rating.

One-star ratings at Southern Water, Thames Water, South West Water and Yorkshire Water were all confirmed by the Environment Agency on Thursday.

This means they will now be blocked from paying executive bonuses as part of a government crackdown launched last year that seeks to prevent companies rewarding failure.

The latest ratings were confirmed as part of the agency’s annual performance review. The best possible rating is four stars, which was only achieved by Severn Trent.

The agency announced on Thursday that pollution incidents are still far too high across the UK, with six category 1 incidents reported in 2025.

These are incidents deemed to have had a major effect on the environment or on households, and also lead to a ban on bonuses.

Both Severn Trent and Anglian Water were found liable for category 1 incidents in 2025, meaning they will also be barred from handing payouts to their bosses.

Overall, the EA found that there were 74 serious sewage pollution incidents in 2025, only slightly fewer than the 75 in 2024.

Alan Lovell, the chairman of the Environment Agency, said that the companies awarded one-star ratings had fallen “well short of the standards rightly demanded by both us and the public”.

Ministers are now set to visit a number of sites to interrogate companies’ performance.

Dame Angela Eagle, the Environment Secretary, said she will also be looking at options to strengthen the ban on executives’ bonuses.

It follows the first ever joint report from the Environment Agency, Natural Resources Wales, the Drinking Water Inspectorate and Ofwat, which leaves nowhere for underperforming companies to hide.

In total, there were 2,666 sewage and water supply incidents that took place in 2025, with Thames Water responsible for more than any other supplier: 464.

That was down from 2,801 in 2024.

James Wallace, the chief executive of River Action, said: “Another year, another record low.

“In 2025 almost every water company in England has been ranked as performing poorly, and the sewage kept flowing into our rivers just as it has done for years.

“This year’s figures show that performance is getting worse, not better.”

PM vows to introduce more ‘public control’

Mr Wallace said the latest pollution figures are further evidence that Thames Water, which released 108,000 hours of raw sewage into Britain’s waterways last year, should be put into special administration.

The latest pollution failures have emerged despite £5bn of investment from water companies, which has pushed households’ bills.

The figures come at a critical moment for the water industry after Andy Burnham vowed to introduce more “public control” over the sector.

A spokesman for Water UK, which represents the sector, admitted that improvements were needed.

He said: “Today’s report shows the lowest level of leakage in history. However, the fact remains that the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough.”

Dame Angela said: “Water companies have let the public down time and time again, and today’s report is further proof that root-and branch reform cannot wait.

“People are sick of excuses. I am demanding answer from the companies that are failing.”

data.title: British baked beans ‘under threat from Burnham tariffs’
data.description:
British baked beans are under threat from Andy Burnham’s decision to cut tariffs on imported food, manufacturers have warned.

On Tuesday, the Government announced the suspension of tariffs on more than 100 food products, including cutting the 16 per cent levy on tinned beans.

The move was part of a package of measures the Chancellor announced in his Budget to give families “breathing space” amid the cost of living crisis.

However, British food bosses have warned that cheap exports from the US and China could undermine the country’s major bean processing industry.

The Heinz baked bean plant in Wigan, Greater Manchester, employs up to 850 people and produces 1.5 million tins a day. The Princes Group, which makes Branston baked beans, is owned by Italian food conglomerate Newlat and is one of Britain’s biggest food manufacturers with around 2,000 UK staff.

Karen Betts, chief executive of the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), said Mr Healey’s Budget had done “nothing to ease the pressures food and drink manufacturers are under”.

“One of the Chancellor’s flagship announcements, removing tariffs from some food and drink products, will have no meaningful impact on consumer prices,” she said.

“But it will undermine British factories and their workers, grappling with much higher costs, producing the same products.”

A spokesman for the Princes Group said: “Based on our understanding of the proposals so far, removing tariffs on imported finished baked beans is unlikely to have a meaningful impact on prices, particularly as there are currently no tariffs on the imported haricot beans used by UK manufacturers and no tariffs on EU imports.

“We believe measures that help address the higher costs of manufacturing food in the UK, particularly energy costs, would have a greater impact for both consumers and British businesses.”

The tariff announcement was made days after the Prime Minister said he would put the British family favourite in his emergency box in case of a national disaster. Asked what items he would stockpile, he picked baked beans, soup and Twiglets.

The FDF said it was also concerned about the lifting of tariffs on boiled sweets, toffees and caramels and pressed sweets like Love Hearts and Parma Violets, as well as chocolate.

Last year, the UK and US both applied a tariff of up to a 10 per cent on chocolate imports from the other country. Since then, the US has increased its tariff to 20 per cent and the UK has just removed it for most products.

In addition, the FDF said there were concerns around jams, marmalades and purees, tomato ketchup, tomato sauces, soups and broths.

“Food and drink manufacturing should be central to the Government’s growth and reindustrialisation agenda,” said Ms Betts. “But time and again, we are treated as an afterthought.

“The Treasury, in particular, has persistently failed to recognise the importance of food and drink manufacturing to jobs and prosperity across the length and breadth of the UK.”

The FDF said that particular companies that could be affected, including confectioners Nestle in York and Halifax, Haribo in Bradford, and Cadbury in Bourneville and Tiptree jam in Colchester.

The Government says the tariff suspensions, taken together with others announced earlier this year, will reduce consumer costs by up to £595m a year, saving households up to £21 on their annual food shop.

In its response to a consultation on the changes, the Government said it recognised there “may be some limited impacts on domestic producers of goods”, but said it “considers the benefits of this to consumers, through reduced costs, outweigh those risks”.

data.title: ‘Millionaire row’ neighbours in court battle over basement cinema
data.description:
Neighbours on a “millionaire’s row” are locked in a High Court battle over plans to build a basement cinema and gym under their garden.

Acting on behalf of the house’s freehold and residents’ group, directors Piers Calvert and Lisa Erickson are fighting against the owner of the ground-floor flat who unveiled plans for the basement beneath the garden of their shared building in west London.

They live in a five-storey Grade II-listed Victorian house in Holland Park, where flats recently sold for more than £3m, which sits in the vicinity of homes belonging to celebrities such as the Beckhams, Sir Elton John and Robbie Williams.

Mr Calvert, a photographer, and Mrs Erickson, a choral singer and former banker, are carrying out the dispute through 51 Holland Park Residents Ltd against Montana International Properties Ltd, an offshore entity of which few details are public.

Sitting at London’s High Court, Master Francesca Kaye must rule whether the company owns only the surface of the garden, or the soil beneath it “to the centre of the earth”.

The freehold company argues that, despite having planning permission for the basement, Montana International has no right to dig deep enough to build the room as the soil beneath the surface of the garden goes beyond the limits of the property.

David Nicholls, the barrister for 51 Holland Park, said: “The demise of the garden [the specific area the company owns] does not carry with it the subsoil to the centre of the earth or to any level beyond that reasonably required for use as a garden.

“The subsoil at 20ft or 100ft or 1,000ft below the surface cannot properly be said to be ‘garden’.”

Mr Calvert owns the lease on the attic flat, while Mrs Erickson, 69, owns the lease on the maisonette below.

Since 2014, the lease on the final flat, which covers the ground and lower ground floors as well as the garden, has been owned by Jersey-listed Montana International Properties Ltd, the owners of which lawyers have refused to reveal.

Planning permission for the 2.5m-deep basement beneath the garden, which also includes a shower room and storage space, was granted to the company in 2018.

Mr Nicholls told Master Kaye: “In short, 51 Holland Park contends that the demise includes the subsoil beneath the garden to no greater depth than is reasonably required for the use of the garden as a garden.”

He added: “There is a presumption that applies particularly to freehold conveyances, namely that the owner of land is presumed to own everything up to the sky and down to the centre of the earth.

“But that presumption does not automatically apply in the leasehold context. The correct starting point is the lease, the actual words used, and the overall context.”

Mr Nicholls said the word “garden” had featured in Montana International’s lease for the property, rather than something that might be thought to include what is under the surface such as “land”.

Lease ‘naturally includes’ subsoil

Daniel Dovar, the barrister for Montana International, argued that in a “plain and natural” reading of the company’s lease, the company’s ownership of the garden extended below the ground “without limitation”.

“The demise is of the whole garden, which naturally includes all the subsoil. There is no lease which provides any alternative construction,” he told the judge.

He continued: “If that were not sufficient, then there is the legal presumption that a conveyance of property includes the airspace above and the subsoil below.”

After three days in court, Master Kaye reserved her decision on the dispute until a later date.

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: Exposed: Britain’s shoddy new-build epidemic
data.description:
Have you bought a new-build home with defects? Do you regret your purchase? Get in touch at money@telegraph.co.uk*.

“I can already point out five issues with this house,” Tom Britton says within a few seconds of stepping out of the car. “And that’s without going into the state of the pavement, the road... and look at this grass.”

Britton and his specialist surveying team are here to root out snags in a brand new home in Corby, Northamptonshire. But from the outset, they are less than impressed.

He squats and pulls up some of the front garden, rubbing a crumbling mixture of tarmac and soil between his fingers. The grass is dead, leaving behind an ugly brown strip.

“That’s not because we’ve had a drought. That will never grow because they’ve laid tarmac underneath,” Britton says wearily. Every house along the new street has the same issue.

Charlie Jones, a first-time buyer, has lived in the property barely a week. Yet despite the property having been built by a “five-star” developer, Britton’s team at new-build inspection company HomeSnag expects to encounter a litany of issues.

“We’ve been to new homes worth as much as £4m that have had problems,” says Britton, who estimates that just 5-10pc of the properties he inspects meet the housebuilding industry’s standard for genuine five-star build quality.

The data his team has collected across 2,000 inspections make for disturbing reading: 70pc of new homes have uneven ceilings, 60pc have ventilation issues and half lack sufficient loft insulation.

Incredibly, nearly a third have mould, including the one we visit. Marius Neculaes, one of 14 surveyors at HomeSnag, discovers it after pulling down panelling under the kitchen units. “That would start to really smell in a few months,” he says.

Some homes have even posed serious safety risks to Britton’s surveyors, including gas and carbon monoxide leaks, live exposed cables and loose brickwork.

Labour has promised to drive a housebuilding revolution, with 1.5 million new homes by 2029. But many of the homes being churned out are blighted by defects.

For those who have paid a premium to avoid the draughty rooms and faulty boilers that often plague older properties, it can prove deeply disheartening.

Jones, who is 28, says a large part of the reason he and his partner forked out £310,000 for a home on a new-build estate was for the “peace of mind” that came with buying box-fresh.

“You’re in your house all the time, so there’s going to be a timescale of when you’re going to start to find faults,” he says. “But you expect a brand new property to not have those for at least 10, 15 years-plus.”

Yet when the report from Britton’s survey comes back, it raises dozens of issues with the house, several of which are flagged as “significant”, including uneven ceilings and a missing extractor fan in the utility room. There are eight defects identified on the roof alone.

HomeSnag’s Britton, who says the average new home has around 130 defects, is indignant.

“This is supposed to be a five-star builder. They know they’re cutting corners, but they rely on the fact most homeowners won’t know what they’re looking for. They’re only looking for cosmetic issues, like marks on the wall.”

Owners typically have two years from the date of completion to flag issues of any size to their developer. After that, there is a further eight-year window in which the builder is no longer responsible but homeowners can appeal to warranty providers who serve as a form of insurance.

Steve Turner, at industry body the Home Builders Federation (HBF), says that this gives new-build homeowners a distinct advantage over those moving into existing housing stock where “if the roof’s leaking, you’ve got to pay for it”.

Yet in the past, warranty providers and housebuilders have been accused of being inextricably linked, raising questions about the independence of decisions over compensation and remediation.

‘Not much quality control’

Housebuilders have faced an onslaught of rising costs in recent years. The average cost of constructing a low-rise house has jumped by £76,000 since 2020, with the soaring price of materials and labour responsible for around half of that increase, according to the HBF.

To keep a lid on bills, volume developers have historically relied heavily on subcontracting. The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (Rics) estimates that around 85-90pc of all construction work is subcontracted, rather than relying on in-house staff.

While site managers are expected to ensure a minimum standard of quality, Jeremy Gray, at the Federation of Master Builders, a trade body for SME builders, says ad-hoc training on sites raises the potential for problems.

“[The volume builders] have got quite a few apprentices coming in, they train them on the edge of the site in these sheds, and then there’s not much quality control. It’s all speed, because the money’s in the land, it’s not really in the houses.”

This, he says, differs from smaller housebuilders where reputation is everything and in-house staff are more common.

Rics identifies subcontracting as a risk when building new homes, warning that “main contractors lose a degree of management and control over specialist work”.

However, Turner, at the HBF, which represents housebuilders, dismisses the idea that subcontracting is to blame for defects.

“New-builds aren’t like cars – they’re not made in factories,” he says. “They’re built in fields, in all weathers, by numerous trades over a period of time. Everything in each different new-build is in some respect different. So you do sometimes get relatively minor snags.”

Britton is more sceptical, believing that builders intentionally cut corners where they believe they can get away with it. “They’re dealing with plots, rather than people,” he says. “It’s a faceless process.”

Help to Buy 2.0

More than half of the British public believe older homes are better quality than new-builds, according to a survey by the Chartered Institute of Builders (CIOB), while almost a third describe new housing as “poor quality”.

There are fears in the sector that Labour’s dogged pursuit of headline delivery figures will only exacerbate this issue at a time when sales of new-builds are already at rock bottom.

“It’s imperative that we stop thinking of housing just in terms of raw delivery, because when you get the product right, you stimulate the market demand,” says David Parry, at the CIOB.

Andy Burnham’s recent announcement about a revived Help to Buy-style scheme – called Your First Home – answered long-held calls from developers for state-led buyer support.

While naturally this has been welcomed by the housebuilding industry, there are concerns about a repeat of the fallout from the previous scheme, in which a rush to build resulted in severe structural and cosmetic defects in new homes.

This led to the creation of industry bodies the New Homes Quality Board (NHQB) and New Homes Ombudsman, which set a more exacting code for housebuilders and allowed homeowners to more easily challenge problems, with the threat of fines if developers failed to respond in good time.

The Ombudsman received 1,800 complaints last year, up from 593 the year before.

However, Turner warns that despite continual promises from the Government, signing up to these regulators is still voluntary.

Earlier this week, the NHQB wrote an open letter to the Government, signed by a number of housebuilders including Vistry, urging the code to be made statutory, with the NHQB chief saying “quality must keep pace with quantity”.

Meanwhile, back in Corby, first-time buyer Jones is just relieved to have called in the professional help of Britton and his team when he did. Once he sends HomeSnag’s report to the developer, as paid-up members of the NHQB, it will have an obligation to remediate the snags within a few weeks.

Only then will Jones and his partner be able to enjoy the home they have worked so hard to pay for.

data.title: British organic food supplier to Riverford hit by fridges hack
data.description:
An organic British food supplier to retailers including Whole Foods and Riverford has fallen victim to a spate of fridge hacks that has hit supermarkets across Europe.

Langridge Organic revealed that hackers took control of six out of 10 cold-room systems, ramping temperature up to 66c and activating defrost cycles.

The attack is the latest in a string of fridge and freezer hacks across at least seven European countries, including Sweden, France and Finland in recent weeks.

At Langridge Organic, in Feltham, west London, hackers had also disabled automatic warnings intended to alert staff to temperatures exceeding safe levels.

Alex Pearce, the managing director of Langridge Organic, told The Grocer: “It was amazing how many parameters they’d changed. It was like kids put in front of a mixing desk: how many levers can we move to the wrong place?”

Mr Pearce said he discovered the incident at 5.30am on Monday, when two units appeared to be malfunctioning, and a third began defrosting.

Suspecting he was witnessing a live cyber-attack, Mr Pearce disconnected the fridges from the internet.

He also told the BBC: “I reckon I caught them by luck right in the middle of it being hacked.”

The wholesaler avoided losing any food, as staff carry out frequent temperature checks.

More than 100 shops across Europe suffered similar cyber attacks on Monday, forcing them to throw away food worth hundreds of thousands of euros.

Refrigeration systems using the software technology Dixell, which is owned by US tech firm Copeland, have been implicated in multiple hacks, with several British meat suppliers using the system reporting cyber-attacks overnight on Monday.

Mr Pearce said he was unclear why the vulnerability exposed in France weeks ago still existed within the systems.

He told The Telegraph: “There is still the broader question of why, after what happened in France last month, the vulnerability still existed with the Dixell Xweb platform.

“We have not been directly contacted by anyone from Copeland to make us aware of any potential risk.”

He added that Langridge Organic has since left the system unplugged until they decide “the next course of action”.

Mr Pearce said: “Thankfully for us this does not have any effect on our ability to function and keep our customers supplied with high-quality organic fruit and vegetables.”

It follows warnings from Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), that Britain’s entire food supply chain is at risk.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Mr Horne said: “We’ve been working through the night alerting organisations where we can see they’ve got exposed technology that is vulnerable in this way.”

Mr Horne said it was too early to say who was behind the attacks, which have coincided with several flights across Europe being grounded by bomb threats.

The NCSC, an arm of GCHQ, said on Tuesday it was aware of “instances where vulnerable technology has been exploited in the UK”.

UK officials have insisted that only a small number of companies have become victims in the attacks.

It is thought that the UK’s major supermarkets have not been affected.

The hacks in France in October also affected fridges supplied by Danish engineering giant Danfoss. In response to the attacks, Danfoss has said that most of the affected fridges were either older systems or newer ones running on outdated software.

A Copeland spokesman acknowledged that “certain XWEB monitoring solutions are impacted by the reported cybersecurity vulnerability”, and said: “As part of our response, we have re-communicated the recommended patching and security protocols to ensure customers have the latest guidance to protect against the identified threats.

“We are proactively engaging with customers and will continue to provide relevant guidance as appropriate.”

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.description:
If you have a notice savings account, you’ll be required to notify your bank or building society a specified number of days ahead of making a withdrawal, detailing how much you want to withdraw. This notice period, set by the bank, has to pass before your funds are released.

Notice periods can range from seven days to 180, but the most common are 30, 60 and 90 days. It’s important to choose an account with a notice period that suits you, as it can be a long wait to get your money.

In theory, your patience is rewarded with higher interest rates than you would get with easy- or instant-access savings accounts. But this isn’t always the case, so you should always do some research before committing to a new account.

In this guide, Telegraph Money addresses:

  • How we determine the best rates
  • What are the best notice savings accounts for November?
  • Expert opinion: Things to consider when choosing a notice savings account
  • How do notice savings accounts work?
  • Verdict: are notice savings accounts worth it?
  • Notice savings account FAQs

How we determine the best rates

The data in these tables is provided by Savings Data Limited and is compiled using automated tracker tools and updates from savings providers. Savings Data Limited then manually checks the information and enters it into a database that feeds the live tables, which update daily.

The savings accounts shown are protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme. The information in this article is intended for information purposes and should not be taken as endorsement or advice.

What are the best notice savings accounts for November?

Use the table below to discover the best notice savings accounts available.

If you decide you don’t want to wait to withdraw your cash, see our guide to the best easy-access accounts. Opting for one of the best current accounts is another way to earn interest while maintaining full access to your money.

Or, if you’d prefer to lock in a guaranteed rate for the next 12 months or more, don’t miss our guide to the best fixed-rate bonds.

For a host of tax-efficient savings options, make sure you check our guide to the best cash Isas.

Expert opinion: Things to consider when choosing a notice savings account

Caitlyn Eastell, of analysts Moneyfactscompare.co.uk, said: “Typically, notice accounts pay a higher rate of interest than easy-access accounts with the benefit of being able to add funds in the account once it’s been opened.

“But an important factor to consider is many providers won’t allow any withdrawals before the end of the notice period and, on the rare occasion earlier access is allowed, may result in a loss of interest.”

Mark Hicks, of investment and savings platform Hargreaves Lansdown, said: “They’re one of the more complicated structures in the savings market. Quite often people don’t realise that they cannot get money out immediately, so they’re saving into a notice account and all of a sudden, they urgently need the money.”

How do notice savings accounts work?

Notice accounts work in a very similar way to easy-access accounts; the difference comes when you want to withdraw money.

Instead of requesting a withdrawal that’s paid out instantly, instead you’ll only receive the money after the requisite notice period – as mentioned, this is commonly 30, 60 or 90 days but there are all sorts of options on the market.

Once the notice period is over, your money will be released.

Verdict: are notice savings accounts worth it?

Notice savings accounts can be worth it if you can plan your savings withdrawals well in advance. In theory, you should receive higher interest rates to make up for the inconvenience, and can usually have unlimited access to your funds – granted, after a bit of a wait.

You can also make ongoing deposits. Unlike some accounts that only accept a single initial deposit, notice accounts allow you to continue adding to your savings whenever you like. Generally, savings will still earn interest during the notice period, but this is worth checking.

For new savers, the notice period may help with money management and preventing impulse buying.

Notice savings account FAQs

Yes, you can withdraw money from the account, but you’ll need to wait until the notice period passes to receive it. This commonly varies from 30 to 180 days.

Some accounts may impose limits on the number of withdrawals that can be made, while others may have a minimum deposit requirement you’ll need to bear in mind – it is worth checking the account’s terms and conditions to find out.

The biggest disadvantage of a notice account is having to wait for a set amount of time before being able to access your funds, which could be an issue if you need money at short notice.

A notice savings account generally allows you to make an unlimited number of deposits and withdrawals, the only catch is that when you want to access your money you have to wait a certain number of days for it to be paid out.

A regular savings account, meanwhile, tends to include terms that require or reward regular deposits – this might be every month, or a certain number of times over the course of a year. You’re often rewarded with higher rates of interest if you can stick to the required deposits, but you may only be able to pay in a certain amount, and withdrawals might be restricted.

data.title: Where to put £100k savings right now for the highest return
data.description:
Have you got a savings strategy to maximise your returns? We want to hear from you. Email money@telegraph.co.uk

The great savings rate decline may not happen this year, as conflict in Iran has halted plans for further Bank Rate reductions. While this is good news for your savings, it’s tempered by the fact that inflation is expected to rise, which can eat away at your returns.

To protect your money, it’s worth putting some effort into finding the accounts paying the best rates possible.

But with so many to choose from, all with differing rates and conditions, finding the best home for your cash can be difficult. Everyone’s circumstances are different: some can afford to lock cash away for years, while others only feel comfortable if they can make instant withdrawals in case of emergencies.

Telegraph Money asked Katie Horne of Flagstone, a cash deposit platform, to give her views on three scenarios that represent common questions we get asked by readers.

For simplicity’s sake, we have not considered tax. In reality, tax on savings interest would be a problem for any money held outside an Isa.

Once you earn interest over £1,000 a year (for most basic-rate taxpayers) or £500 (for higher-rate payers), returns are subject to income tax, due to the personal savings allowance.

Scenario 1

A retired couple in their 70s with £100,000 in cash. They are happy to lock up £80,000 for more than a year, but need access to the rest – though not necessarily daily

Katie says: “The retired couple could take advantage of some longer-term fixed accounts, specifically the Chetwood Bank 12-month Fixed Term Deposit, which pays 5.13pc.

“They can place £80,000 into this product, earning themselves interest of £4,104 a year. If they are comfortable securing a longer fixed term, and concerned that rates might be significantly lower in 12 months’ time, another option is Chetwood Bank’s 5 Year Fixed Term Deposit, paying 5.11pc AER, which would generate £4,088 a year in interest.

“For the remaining £20,000, they could use their Isa allowance – Aldermore Bank Instant Access Cash Isa pays 3.77pc AER, generating interest of £754 a year.

“However, if they have used their Isa allowance, they could choose the Al Rayan Bank instant access account, paying an expected profit rate of 4.11pc, earning £822.

“All of these accounts would be covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS). This balanced portfolio would meet their near-term liquidity requirements and generate a blended interest rate of 4.84pc to 4.93pc, equivalent to between £4,842 and £4,926 a year.”

Scenario 2

A working woman in her 50s with £100,000 in cash. She needs ready access to £80,000 but can lock up £20,000 for up to three years

Katie says: “She could opt to place £80,000 into an instant-access account from Al Rayan Bank, which pays an expected profit rate of 4.11pc.

“This account allows unlimited withdrawals without any restrictions and would earn her £3,288 in interest a year.

“If she is willing to restrict access somewhat, she could achieve a slightly higher rate with Perenna Bank’s three-month fixed term product, currently paying 4.21pc AER, earning £3,368 in interest a year.

“For the remaining £20,000, she could secure the Chetwood Bank 3 Year Fixed Term Deposit, currently paying 5pc, earning £1,000 a year in interest. Alternatively, she could lock in for a shorter period and secure a slightly higher rate of 5.13pc with the Chetwood Bank 12 Month Fixed Term Deposit, earning £1,026 a year.

“Her selection here would probably be driven how much she values certainty versus flexibility. Fixing for longer provides certainty over the rate she’ll receive, while a shorter term would allow her to reassess sooner as the interest rate environment evolves.

“This balanced portfolio would meet her near-term liquidity requirements and generate a blended interest rate of 4.29pc to 4.39pc, or £4,288 to £4,394, again covered by the FSCS.”

Scenario 3

A working man in his 40s. Has no savings, but can put aside £1,500 a month for the next five years. Doesn’t need access for five years

Katie says: “A number of big banks offer good savings rates with specific requirements. For example, Santander Edge Saver offers 6pc AER with a minimum deposit of £1 and a maximum deposit of £4,000, or £233 a year in interest. Once his savings have grown, he can reassess and diversify his investments.

“We would also suggest that he look into cash Isas to take advantage of the tax-free status. You can currently invest up to £20,000 in Isas each year without paying tax on the interest you earn.

“The best rates over the past 12 months have been around the 4.5pc mark. Currently, Trading 212 offers a cash Isa at 4.87pc with no minimum required. If he puts in £300 a month, he’ll get a return of £94 a year.”

Scenario 4

A saver in their 60s with £100,000 in cash. They don’t need access to all of this money immediately, but want to generate a steady return while keeping some flexibility

Katie says: “For savers who want to strike a balance between flexibility and income, laddering fixed-term deposits can be a really effective strategy. It allows you to earn higher returns on money you don’t need straight away, while keeping some accessible in case of emergencies.

“In this example, £25,000 could be held in an easy access account with Al Rayan Bank, paying an expected profit rate of 4.11pc, earning £1,027.50.

“A further £25,000 could be placed in a six-month fixed term account with ABC International Bank, paying 4.57pc AER, earning £1,142.50 in interest over the year.

“For the next portion, £25,000 could be locked into a 12-month fixed term deposit from Chetwood Bank, paying 5.13pc, which would generate £1,282.50 in annual interest.

“The final £25,000 could go into a 24-month fixed term deposit from Chetwood Bank, paying 5pc AER, earning £1,250 a year.

“This combination would provide access to a portion of funds at all times, while maintaining steady income from staggered maturities. It also ensures full FSCS protection across four banks, a key advantage of spreading deposits.

“Altogether, this portfolio would achieve an average blended rate of 4.7pc, generating around £4,703 in annual interest, with funds maturing every six to 12 months to allow reinvestment at new market rates.”

data.title: Silicon Valley investor shuts London office as US dominates AI
data.description:
One of Silicon Valley’s most successful venture-capital firms has shut down its London office as the US dominates a tidal wave of multibillion-dollar AI deals.

Sequoia Capital, which opened a UK office in 2020 and hired a string of partners at the height of the post-pandemic tech boom, said it would cut jobs and shift its focus to the West Coast of America.

The firm said: “We are closing our London office, which means several people will be leaving Sequoia. We simply don’t see the need for a local presence.”

The venture-capital business, which has around $80bn (£60bn) in assets and is known for early investments in Apple and Google, said it was pulling back after an “expansionary phase” during which it opened offices around the world.

It previously withdrew from its Chinese and Indian ventures, spinning them off into separate businesses focused on Asia.

The firm said it would continue to invest in British and European founders with “world-class support from our home base in the Bay Area”.

Yet the decision represents a setback for Britain’s AI ambitions and its attempts to attract major global investors.

It comes as dealmaking in Silicon Valley reaches record levels as venture investors compete to sign cheques for promising AI labs. Total US venture funding has topped $500bn so far this year, already outstripping the $340bn raised in 2025.

UK start-ups have also enjoyed a series of bumper funding rounds, with more than $23.4bn raised in 2026, according to DealRoom data. Yet the level of funding and the size of the UK start-up scene remains far smaller than the US.

Sequoia’s withdrawal from London followed a similar retreat by Andreessen Horowitz, which is led by Donald Trump-backing US billionaire Marc Andreessen, in 2025.

The firm had set up in the City to pursue cryptocurrency deals before switching to the US after Mr Trump returned to power in 2025. Coatue, another US venture fund, also quit London in 2024.

Sequoia had hired a series of marquee technology investors to lead its London branch. Yet some of its most successful UK investments were led by partners based in the US, such as an investment in $22bn AI voiceover business ElevenLabs.

The venture firm, which was founded in 1972 by early Apple investor Don Valentine, underwent a major shift last year as Roelof Botha, the managing partner, was pushed out by other senior partners.

Some of Sequoia’s current London partners will move to the US with the firm. Luciana Lixandru, one of its senior London partners, said she would stay in Europe and remain a partner at the firm.

George Robson, another London-based partner, said the firm had chosen to focus on the US “where the pace of change is extraordinary”.

Sequoia was previously chaired by Welsh-born billionaire Sir Michael Moritz, one of Silicon Valley’s most prominent venture investors, before he stepped down in 2023.

data.title: Bank collapse topples Trump ally in Paraguay
data.description:
Paraguay’s president has resigned amid mounting protests after the takeover of a financial institution linked to him left millions of people unable to access their money.

Demonstrations have swept the South American country, with customers demanding the return of their funds after the central bank took control of Ueno on Tuesday, citing a severe capital shortfall.

Within minutes of the resignation of Santiago Peña, a Right-wing ally of Donald Trump, Paraguay’s lower house voted unanimously to impeach him.

“I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed,” he said in a video announcing his decision on X. “It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me.”

Mr Peña, who until last year held a stake in a company related to Ueno, said his priority was “the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system”.

The impeachment came as thousands protested for a third day, as they tried to recoup lost savings, wages and pensions. About three million depositors, including pensioners, lost access to their money.

Long lines of people trying to withdraw cash from Ueno branches snaked down Asuncion’s streets on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Paraguay’s central bank said it took over Ueno owing to a severe capital shortfall, to “protect depositors and preserve the stability of the financial system”.

Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, had more than 60 per cent of Paraguay’s adults on its books.

Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president, who until last year had a stake in Ueno’s holding company, could grow so rapidly and become so important despite repeated warnings about its dubious lending practices.

His own Colorado Party backed the president’s removal on Thursday, and all 78 members of the lower house voted to impeach him.

‘Betrayed, swindled, deceived’

“In the face of these accusations, I can’t pretend to be oblivious,” Alejandro Aquilera, a ruling party deputy, said during the debate.

“We have more than three million Paraguayans who have been harmed, who feel betrayed, swindled, deceived,” she said.

Mr Peña had attempted to ease tensions by requesting the resignation of Carlos Carvallo, the central bank president, who subsequently stepped down.

He also enacted a law that set a limit of five business days to return most of the funds to depositors.

But the measures proved insufficient, with hundreds of demonstrators calling for his removal and clashing with police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd in the capital.

Mr Peña served as finance minister before becoming president in 2023. Pedro Alliana, the vice-president, will now replace him.

Mr Peña’s resignation marks Mr Trump’s latest loss of a South American ally after Flavio Bolsonaro failed to defeat leftist Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s presidential election last month.

It had been hoped that Mr Bolsonaro who later fled to the United States, would pick up the mantle of his father and Trump ally Jair Bolsonaro who lost to Lula in 2022 and was subsequently jailed.

Mr Trump is still reeling from the fallout of this week’s midterm election disaster.

The Republican Party’s substantial losses at the ballot box have left him diminished in Washington and facing tougher legislative oversight and scrutiny of his agenda.

data.title: Anthropic IPO in turmoil as AI sell-off hammers valuation
data.description:
Anthropic’s blockbuster stock market float has been thrown into chaos by a global AI sell-off, with investors considering steep cuts to the company’s valuation.

The Claude developer had been targeting a listing within the next fortnight that would value it at around $1.5tn (£1.1tn).

However, some major investors reportedly now view a value of around $1tn as more realistic after the Democrats’ success in the US midterms triggered a sharp drop in AI shares.

This is alongside concern among analysts that the float could be delayed.

Three funds told the Wall Street Journal that Anthropic’s valuation would need to come down to navigate the sell-off, which saw more than $3tn wiped from US markets on Thursday.

One investor suggested a reduction to roughly $1tn, which is dramatically lower than the $2tn mooted for the company just a few weeks ago.

Concern over Anthropic’s valuation came as a global rout of technology stocks deepened on Friday, driven by fears that the Democrats will slow the AI rollout.

Anthropic had been hoping to go public before Thanksgiving in the US later this month. However, that timeline could now be in doubt.

Richard Windsor, a technology analyst, said: “There is an escalating risk that the IPO gets delayed. It will not be well received in this environment.”

Nalin Patel, an analyst at PitchBook, said: “A postponement would protect against near-term valuation risks and would be more likely if the correction sustains over a longer period.”

The odds of Anthropic launching its float in November plummeted sharply over the past day on Polymarket, a prediction market, with investors now expecting the deal in December.

Anthropic’s proposed deal was already under pressure amid mounting concerns about its spending plans and worries that a surge in its revenues in recent months is starting to cool.

Earlier this week, the AI giant revealed that its spending commitments were heading towards $1tn to help meet growing data centre and computing demands to power its Claude bot.

It also disclosed in filings before its float that it had made a loss of $104bn in the first nine months of the year.

Anthropic was contacted for comment.

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: Troubled housebuilder to shut offices and slash jobs in turnaround scramble
data.description:
Vistry is to shut down half its offices across the country and slash jobs as it grapples with a nationwide property downturn.

The embattled housebuilder said it would close 13 of its 25 offices in a move Adam Daniels, its chief executive, said was “difficult but necessary” as it seeks to save £50m next year.

The company expects its average daily debt pile to swell to £800m in the second half of the year, up from £771m during the same period last year.

It is unclear how many of Vistry’s 4,500 staff are at risk under the changes, which will come into effect in January.

Vistry revealed a record loss of £661m for the first half of the financial year in September, and said it planned to build fewer homes as rising mortgage rates triggered by the Iran war’s impact on inflation dampened demand.

Estate agency Savills expects house prices to fall until at least the second half of 2028, with London, the South East and the East of England worst affected.

The average five-year fixed mortgage rate is currently 5.99pc, according to Moneyfacts - up from 4.96pc at the start of February before Donald Trump ordered the first strikes on Iran.

Vistry blamed its struggles on “difficult” market conditions, nervous home buyers and affordability constraints.

Mr Daniels said the firm had taken “decisive action to create a smaller, more focused and disciplined business”.

Vistry’s share price slumped by more than 4pc to £2.77 on Thursday. Its shares have tumbled by almost 57pc since the start of the year.

Its struggles come despite securing £350m from the Government in August to build affordable and social homes.

Labour had vowed to oversee 1.5m houses being built during this parliament. However, many developers and experts have warned the weak market means the target is effectively dead in the water.

Official figures show that only 306,640 housing starts have taken place across the UK since Labour took power in July 2024. It means Andy Burnham must oversee the construction of nearly 1.2 million more homes by August 2029 at the latest to hit Labour’s target.

The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates today for the first time in three years from 3.75pc to 4pc, adding to the strain on mortgage borrowers.

data.title: VMO2 debt crisis triggers thousands of job cuts
data.description:
Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) has outlined plans to cut thousands of jobs and halt its rollout of fibre broadband as the telecoms giant grapples with an escalating debt crisis.

The telecoms company has warned of significant job cuts as it seeks to ease concerns about its ability to finance £22bn of borrowings.

VMO2 said it would save around £300m through redundancies – equivalent to around a third of its labour costs – as part of a wider cost-cutting programme aimed at saving £800m per year by 2029.

It did not say how many of its 16,000-strong UK workforce would be affected, though Sky News reported last week that around 4,000 jobs would be axed.

The company also said it would stop rolling out upgrades to its full-fibre broadband network in an effort to shore up its balance sheet.

Noel McClean, the deputy general secretary of the Prospect union, described the job cuts as “devastating”. He added: “Industry conditions are tough but this level of cuts will drastically alter the way VMO2 works.”

Other cost-saving measures include reducing the use of contractors and ramping up the deployment of AI. Bosses are also considering whether to scrap this year’s dividend.

VMO2, which is owned by Liberty Global and Telefónica, was formed through a £31bn merger in 2021 that gave it the scale to challenge former state monopoly BT but also loaded the group with debt.

That debt has come under scrutiny in recent months amid fierce competition from start-up broadband rivals and uncertainty over its ability to consolidate the market.

VMO2’s bonds suffered a sell-off over the summer, trading as low as 41p in the pound, in a sign of investor concern.

It comes after the Competition and Markets Authority threatened to block a £2bn takeover of “alt-net” broadband firm Netomnia by VMO2’s parent company.

The watchdog warned the tie-up risked damaging competition and pushing up prices, arguing that rival CityFibre would have instead bought Netomnia.

The intervention prompted a furious response from VMO2, particularly in the light of a government decision to allow BT’s rescue deal for TalkTalk in spite of competition concerns.

VMO2 said it was facing a “paradoxical regulatory direction in fibre that does not reflect economic reality”.

Fibre rethink

After announcing the decision to halt fibre upgrades, bosses argued that there was no economic case for building three overlapping fibre networks in the UK.

It is exploring wholesale agreements with rivals such as BT’s Openreach network in areas it does not already cover.

VMO2 also said it would keep investing in the expansion of its 5G mobile network.

It came as VMO2 revealed it lost 23,000 broadband customers owing to tough competition from rivals, though this was an improvement on the same time last year.

Bosses said they expected both service revenue and profits to decline by between 3pc and 5pc for the full year.

Lutz Schüler, the chief executive of VMO2, said: “Given the market conditions we face, the regulatory backdrop in fibre and the technological changes sweeping across all areas of the economy, standing still and doing what we’ve always done is not an option and while many of these decisions are tough, they are necessary for our future success and growth.

“While we will give a fuller update on the new strategic plan in the coming months, we are already progressing and making difficult decisions to prioritise investments and reduce costs, which includes the size of our workforce.

“This is not something I take lightly, but my commitment to our people is that for those leaving we will treat them fairly and with respect.”

VMO2 is not the only telecoms giant making job cuts, with BT Group and VodafoneThree also pursuing significant redundancies.

BT unveiled plans in 2023 to shed as much as a quarter of its then 130,000-strong workforce by 2030, partly driven by AI.

VodafoneThree announced 1,200 job losses across Europe earlier this year as part of a cost-cutting drive to save £700m annually by 2030.
